rows.answer:
**Short answer:** When a customer's integration exceeds its limit, the API returns **HTTP 429** with a `Retry-After` header giving the number of seconds to wait. Our SDKs honour that header and back off exponentially. I could not find documentation for the 429 response body or for `X-RateLimit-*` headers, so don't promise customers either.

**What the customer gets back**
- HTTP status **429** when a request is over the limit [1].
- A `Retry-After` header with the number of seconds to wait [1].
- Rejected requests don't count against the monthly event quota [1].
- Endpoints the customer's plan doesn't include return **HTTP 403**, not 429 [1].

**How they know when to retry**
- The `Retry-After` value is the documented signal [1]. Our SDKs read it and back off exponentially on their own [1].
- Customers who write their own client should respect `Retry-After`. The sources don't give a backoff schedule or a maximum retry count for custom clients.

**How limits apply**
- Limits are per workspace, not per API key. Ten keys in one workspace share one budget [1].
- Short bursts up to 2x the limit are allowed for 10 seconds [1].
- Limits depend on plan. For example, `POST /v2/events` is 100 req/s on Starter, 2,000 on Growth and 10,000 on Enterprise (default) [1].
- Enterprise ingest limits on `/v2/events` and `/v2/events/batch` can be raised up to 3x the default by contract. Growth limits are fixed by contract [1].
- Temporary raises for a one-off backfill (up to 72 hours) can be granted by the Data Plane on-call primary [1].

**Related: outage responses (not rate limiting)**
- During an ingest outage, the API returns **HTTP 503**. In INC-2291, about 38 million events were rejected this way, and the customer SDKs retried them [2].
- A Python SDK bug that could reorder events when the gateway returned 503 was fixed in September 2026 [5]. This is about 503s, not 429s.

**Gaps and things to confirm**
- The 429 response body format (error code, message fields) isn't documented in the knowledge base.
- `X-RateLimit-*` headers are not documented. Only `Retry-After` is.
- The Engineering rate-limit page says the public docs copy it on each release [1]. I didn't find that public copy, so check it matches before quoting it to customers.
- The Support collection had no customer-facing guidance on 429 handling. Ask Support or the Data Plane team for the approved wording and any custom-client backoff advice.

Sources:
[1] Northwind Pipelines API rate limits by plan (Engineering, updated 2026-10-21)
[2] Postmortem: Ingest outage in us-east cell (INC-2291) (Engineering, 2026-08-14)
[5] Northwind Pipelines changelog: September–October 2026 (Engineering, 2026-10-01)

**Where to ask:** Post your request in `#eng-leads` [1]. The register that tracks codenames is maintained by Mateo Alvarez (Group PM) [1].

**Naming rules:**

- **Internal only.** Codenames must never appear in customer-facing material, release notes or the status page [1].
- **No collisions.** A new codename must not match a production service name, a vendor name or an existing codename [1].
- **Check the lookalikes.** The register flags pairs that are easy to confuse: Sandbar (our EU data residency cell project) is not Saltmarsh, which is a vendor, and Tidepool (Postgres CDC v2) is not Tributary (streaming joins) [1].

**Existing codenames to avoid:**

| Codename | What it is | Status (Oct 28) |
|---|---|---|
| Tributary | Streaming joins | Private beta; GA January 2027 |
| Lantern | Self-serve billing portal | Beta February 2027 |
| Hydrant | Automatic scaling of ingest gateways | Shipped October 22, 2026 |
| Undertow | Payment-provider migration | In progress |
| Sandbar | EU data residency (`eu-central` cell) | Limited availability |
| Tidepool | Postgres CDC v2 | Not picked in cycle 5 |
| Bellbuoy | Email usage alerts | Re-pitch for cycle 6 |
| Wayfinder | Pipeline editor redesign | Discovery |

Retired codenames are Keel (original multi-cell architecture, 2022) and Gannet (runner migration to Graviton, Q3 2026) [1]. The register doesn't say whether retired names can be reused, so ask in `#eng-leads` before picking one.

**Also avoid informal service names.** Slack and incident channels use nicknames such as "the firehose" (`ingest-gateway`), "the attic" (Driftwood) and "the till" (Ledger). These aren't codenames, and they shouldn't be reused for a new project [1].

**Gaps:** The sources don't describe a request form, a turnaround time or who approves a codename. They also don't include a style guide for codename formats. Your `#eng-leads` request will need to cover those points [1].

**Short answer:** Harriet Vance is Ledger's change approver, with Arjun Mehta as delegate. Both are out November 24–27, so for a November 25 sign-off you will probably need the VP Engineering fallback, Dmitri Sokolov, unless one of them arranges cover.

**Who can approve**

- Ledger is owned by Identity & Billing (IDB) and classed Confidential [3].
- Normal changes need sign-off from the change approver of the team that owns the affected service [1]. For IDB, that is Harriet Vance, with Arjun Mehta as delegate [2].
- Head of Security sign-off is only required for normal changes to Restricted services [1]. Ledger is not Restricted [3], so it isn't needed.
- Normal changes include schema migrations, infrastructure configuration, and changes to billing logic [1]. Whatever the change is, it will likely fall into this category.

**Availability on November 25**

- Harriet and Arjun are both out November 24–27 [5].
- If the approver and delegate are both unavailable, the VP Engineering may approve, and the exception is logged in `#eng-changes` [1]. Dmitri Sokolov is VP Engineering [2].
- Arranging cover before they leave is the cleaner route, because it avoids an exception.

**Freezes and timing**

- The month-end billing freeze runs from October 30 until invoices are sent, usually around November 2. It does not cover November 25 [1][5].
- The holiday freeze runs December 18 to January 4, so it does not affect this date [1].
- Deploys are allowed Monday to Thursday, 09:00–16:00 Pacific [11]. November 25, 2026 is a Wednesday, so it falls inside that window.
- Approvals are valid for 7 days. If the change hasn't shipped by then, it must be re-approved [1]. For a November 25 ship date, get sign-off on or after about November 18 so it doesn't lapse, or re-request it if the timing moves.

**Things to check**

- If the change is to the Managed Postgres infrastructure rather than Ledger's own logic, the owning team is Platform (PLAT). Its approver is Oluwaseun Adeyemi, with Kofi Mensah as delegate [2][3].
- The Thanksgiving-week incident commander is Priya Raman [8]. The IC can approve only emergency changes during a declared incident [1], so the IC cannot sign off a normal change.
- The team directory was last updated September 30 [2]. Confirm current approvers in `#eng-changes` before you rely on it.

rows.answer:
**Short answer:** You need sign-off from PLAT's change approver, currently Oluwaseun Adeyemi (delegate: Kofi Mensah). No security sign-off is required.

## Who signs off

- Hydrant is owned by PLAT, while the gateways themselves are owned by DP [1].
- Each cell's floor and ceiling is Hydrant configuration in the PLAT infrastructure repo. Changing one is a normal change and needs sign-off from PLAT's change approver [1][2].
- PLAT's change approver is Oluwaseun Adeyemi, with Kofi Mensah as delegate [8].
- Hydrant stores no customer data and is not a Restricted service, so no security sign-off is needed [1].

## Current us-east ceiling

- us-east runs 16 gateway replicas at the Hydrant floor and 64 at the ceiling. It has 6,240 workspaces as of October 1 [2].

## Approval process

Under the production change approval policy, a normal change follows these steps [7]:

1. Add the `change:normal` label to the PR and fill in the risk and rollback sections of the template.
2. Request review from the approver (or delegate) as a CODEOWNERS reviewer.
3. Approvals are valid for 7 days. If the change hasn't shipped by then, re-request.

Don't use `nwctl scale ingest` by hand. Hydrant reverts manual replica changes within 2 minutes [1]. A `nwctl hydrant hold` pins the replica count for debugging, is a standard change, and lasts at most 4 hours [1]. It is not a way to change the ceiling.

## Check the load before you raise it

Hydrant pages the Data Plane primary on-call if a cell sits at its ceiling for 10 minutes, because hitting the ceiling usually means a gateway problem rather than real traffic [1]. Before asking for a higher ceiling, confirm the traffic is real. us-east was also the cell hit by the August ingest outage (INC-2291) [2][6].

## Vendor contract terms

I found no vendor contract governing Hydrant. The project register lists it as an internal PLAT codename that shipped October 22, 2026 [5], so the approval path above is the only one I found.

Don't confuse this with customer rate limits. Enterprise customers can get their `/v2/events` ingest limits raised up to 3x through a request in the DP queue. DP checks that the customer's cell has gateway headroom before agreeing [3]. That is a separate process from raising the Hydrant ceiling.

**Short answer:** During a declared incident, the incident commander (IC) can approve an emergency change. For Thanksgiving week, the IC is Priya Raman, who normally manages the Data Plane team.

**Who approves**

- The production change policy says emergency changes "may be approved by the incident commander during a declared incident" [1]. The incident FAQ confirms the IC can approve emergency changes, including ones that would normally need the owning team's change approver [2].
- The on-call rota lists Priya Raman as IC for the shift starting Tuesday, November 24, 2026, which is Thanksgiving week [7]. Thanksgiving falls on Thursday, November 26.
- Priya Raman is the Data Plane (DP) engineering manager and DP's named change approver. Her delegate is Lin Zhou [3].
- The rota was last edited October 28. The only IC swaps recorded are for December 8 and 15, so the November 24 entry appears unchanged [7]. The rota notes that PagerDuty is the official record for paging, so confirm the IC there before relying on this.

**After the emergency change**

- The owning team's change approver must review the change retroactively within two business days [1]. If the change touches Data Plane, that is Priya Raman, and she is also the IC for that week. If it touches another team's service, that team's approver reviews it instead [1][3].

**Backup approvers**

- If the approver and delegate are both unavailable, the VP Engineering may approve, and exceptions are logged in `#eng-changes` [1]. The VP Engineering is Dmitri Sokolov [3].
- No documented backup IC exists for Thanksgiving week. I did not find one in the knowledge base.
- Harriet Vance and Arjun Mehta (Identity & Billing) are both out November 24–27 [10]. Harriet is not the IC that week, but if the incident involves billing or Keystone, expect limited IDB coverage. Plan accordingly.

**Holiday rules**

- The only holiday freeze I found runs December 18, 2026 to January 4, 2027, and allows emergency changes [1]. I found no freeze covering Thanksgiving week.
- For Thanksgiving week, US-based on-call engineers may hand overnight hours (22:00–07:00 Pacific) to London-based follow-the-sun cover. This must be arranged with the team lead [7]. This affects paging coverage, not who can approve changes.

rows.answer:
**Short answer:** On the Growth plan ($1,200/month), the bulk endpoint `POST /v2/events/batch` allows **50 requests per second** per workspace, with up to **10,000 events or 10 MB per request**. Those are the standard limits. A one-off backfill can get a temporary raise, but the documents don't say how large it can be.

**Standard limits (Growth)**
- **Rate:** 50 req/s, shared across the whole workspace. Ten API keys in one workspace share one budget [2].
- **Burst:** Short bursts up to 2x the limit (100 req/s) are allowed for 10 seconds [2].
- **Request size:** 10,000 events or 10 MB, whichever applies [2].
- **Over the limit:** The API returns HTTP 429 with a `Retry-After` header. Rejected requests don't count against the monthly event quota [2]. The SDKs back off automatically [2].

**Backfill exceptions**
- A temporary raise for a one-off backfill can be granted on any plan that has the endpoint. It lasts up to 72 hours and is approved by the Data Plane on-call primary [2].
- Growth limits are otherwise fixed by contract. For more capacity, the documents point to Enterprise, where ingest limits can be raised up to 3x the default by contract [2].
- The documents don't give the size of a backfill raise, and they don't say how to request one beyond going through the Data Plane on-call. Check with the Data Plane team before promising the customer a specific rate.

**Retention: check the one-year window**
- Default archive retention is now 365 days (reduced from 400) [7]. Archived events older than that are deleted by lifecycle rules [7].
- Backfilling exactly one year of history puts the oldest events right at that boundary. Any data older than 365 days would be removed.
- Enterprise customers can contract for archive retention up to 730 days, with security team approval [7]. Growth customers can't go past 400 days without that approval [1].

**Quota**
- The Growth plan includes 100 million events per month, with overage at $8 per additional million [1]. A large backfill will count against this, so check the customer's expected volume before the run.

- Hydrant itself is owned by Platform, but the gateways are owned by Data Plane [3].

**The November 17 rota**

| Role | Person |
|---|---|
| Data Plane primary (paged for a ceiling alert) | Tom Whitfield [1] |
| Data Plane secondary (paged if primary doesn't ack in 10 min) | Ines Duarte [1][2] |
| Platform primary | Jonas Feld [1] |

| Incident commander | Oluwaseun Adeyemi [1] |

The Platform primary is paged for a different Hydrant failure, when the controller is down, not for a ceiling. The Platform team is not paged for a ceiling alert [3].

**Escalation if it becomes an incident**

- The runbook's severity levels still apply. A full outage of ingest or pipelines for a cell is SEV-1, which requires an immediate page, an incident declared, and an IC assigned within 15 minutes [2].

- The runbook's "Ingest 5xx rate above 1%" steps still apply. Check which cell is affected and look at gateway TLS handshake errors first [3].
- Don't run `nwctl scale ingest` by hand. Hydrant reverts manual changes within 2 minutes. To pin the replica count, use `nwctl hydrant hold`, which lasts at most 4 hours [3].

- The rota was last edited October 28. Its listed swaps cover November 10 and the December IC weeks, not November 17 [1]. PagerDuty is the record for paging, so confirm there before relying on this. Swaps should be made in `#oncall-swaps` and reflected in PagerDuty before the shift starts [1][2].

- I found no vendor or external support contact that handles Hydrant escalations. Hydrant paging goes to internal engineering [1][3].

The first response is due within **2 hours**, 24/7, under the current support SLA.

**Plan:** The plan with 100 million included events a month is Growth ($1,200/month) [1].

**Severity:** Production pipelines being down, or events not being ingested for the workspace, is defined as P1 (Critical) [4]. A customer-reported pipeline outage fits that definition. The customer picks the priority when opening the ticket, but Support may change it after triage and must tell the customer why [2].

**Deadline:** The current Growth P1 targets (effective August 1, 2026, and applying to tickets opened on or after that date) are [4]:

| Item | Growth P1 |
|---|---|
| First response | 2 hours |
| Update cadence | Every 4 hours |
| Coverage | 24/7 |

The 2025 edition listed 4 hours for this case, but the August 2026 edition replaced it [4]. Because coverage is 24/7, weekends and public holidays don't extend the deadline. Business-hours exclusions apply only to the non-P1 priorities [4].

**Clock start and channels:** The sources say that tickets are tracked in the helpdesk, and that tickets can be opened by email or through the help center [2][4]. Slack Connect messages do not start an SLA clock [2][4]. The sources don't spell out any other rule for when the clock starts, so I can't say more than that.

**Other points:**
- If the outage affects more than one workspace, the support process says to declare an incident with `/incident declare`. Incident severity is set by the incident process, not by the ticket priority [4].
- The sources describe service credits only for missed Enterprise P1 first responses, not Growth [4]. Growth customers get no credit for a missed P1 response under these sources.

Four endpoints are unavailable on Starter workspaces. The internal rate-limit reference lists them as "Not available" for Starter, and calls to them return HTTP 403, not a rate-limit response [1].

| Endpoint | Purpose | Starter status |
|---|---|---|
| `POST /v2/events/batch` | Bulk backfill and replays | Not available [1] |
| `POST /v2/reference-tables/{id}/refresh` | Force an Enrich snapshot rebuild | Not available [1] |

The SCIM endpoints are also unavailable on Growth. Only Enterprise can use them, at 20 req/s [1].

Starter workspaces can still call the other endpoints in that table, but with lower limits. For example, they can use `POST /v2/events` at 100 req/s, `GET /v2/pipelines` at 10 req/s, and `POST /v2/pipelines/{id}/runs` at 1 req/s [1]. The legacy `POST /v1/track` endpoint is also open to Starter at 50 req/s, but it stops accepting events on April 30, 2027 [1][7].

Two points to be aware of:

- **Audit log export:** The changelog describes audit log export as a feature admins can use from Settings → Security [7]. That entry doesn't mention plan limits. The rate-limit reference is the only source that says the API endpoint is unavailable on Starter [1]. I didn't find a document that explains the gap between the UI and the API.
- **Source scope:** The rate-limit page was last updated October 21, 2026, and is described as the internal source of truth [1]. I found no separate Starter-specific document or public API docs that list these restrictions.

**Answer: 30 minutes.** For a P1 ticket from a standard Enterprise customer (no Premium Support), the first response is due within 30 minutes, 24/7, with updates every hour [1]. This is the 2026 edition, effective August 1, 2026, which applies to tickets opened on or after that date [1]. The 2025 edition set this at 1 hour, and that target is superseded [1][2].

**Response targets for comparison**

| Plan | Priority | First response | Update cadence | Coverage |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Enterprise | P1 | 30 minutes | Every hour | 24/7 |
| Enterprise + Premium Support | P1 | 15 minutes | Every 30 minutes | 24/7, TAM joins the call |

[1]

**Premium Support changes the P1 commitment**

Premium Support halves the P1 first-response target to 15 minutes and adds a named technical account manager who joins the call [1]. It is only sold with Enterprise, costs $24,000 per year or 10% of the annual contract value (whichever is higher), and cannot be added to Growth [1].

**Consequences of a missed target**

If we miss the first-response target on an Enterprise P1 ticket, the customer gets a credit of 5% of that month's fee per miss, capped at 25% per month. Account teams request these and Support Operations approves them. They are separate from availability SLA credits under the 99.95% commitment [1].

**Clock rules and definitions**

- P1 means production pipelines are down, or events are not being ingested, for the customer's workspace [1].
- Slack Connect messages do not start an SLA clock. Tickets go through the help center or to support@northwind.example. Enterprise customers can also page Support by phone for P1 issues [1].
- Because P1 coverage is 24/7, the business-hours definition (08:00–18:00, Monday–Friday, in the customer's region) does not change the P1 deadline [1].
- If a P1 affects more than one workspace, the engineer declares an incident with `/incident declare`. Severity is set by the incident process, not by ticket priority [1].

**Gap:** The documents I found do not say exactly when the 30-minute timer starts (for example, ticket creation versus the first page or email). I'd confirm that with Support Operations before quoting the deadline to a customer.

**Direct answer: 45 minutes.** A deploy sits in the canary cell for 45 minutes before it can be promoted automatically [2]. The engineering handbook still says 20 minutes [1], but the October 9 pipeline change note supersedes it for deploys started on or after October 12, 2026 [2]. The note says the handbook will be edited to match, so it may be stale until then [2].

**Does the bake vary?** Not by service or risk level in these sources. The 45 minutes applies to every deploy. What differs is what happens after canary:
- Most services go to all cells at once after the bake [2].
- Changes under `ingest/` or `runner/` (data-plane deploys) roll out in waves: canary → `us-central` → `us-west` → `us-east` → `eu-central`, with 30 minutes between waves [2].
- A typical non-data-plane change reaches all production cells about 50 minutes after merge, versus about 25 before. A data-plane change takes about two and a half hours to reach every cell [2].

**Conditions for automatic promotion after the bake**
- Error rate and p95 latency stay within 10% of the baseline. This is unchanged from before [2][1].
- Zero sustained TLS handshake errors between gateways and brokers in canary [2].
- Runner consumer lag does not grow by more than 2 minutes during the bake [2].

You can check these in Lookout's "Canary analysis" panel, which shows each check's value against its threshold [2]. `nwctl deploy status` shows which checks a deploy has passed and how long until its next wave [2].

**Holds and overrides**
- **Hold:** anyone can run `/deploy hold <deploy-id>` in Slack. The deploy stays in canary until someone runs `/deploy release` or rolls it back [2]. This is the way to extend the bake indefinitely.
- **Expedite (skip the bake):** the incident commander can approve `/deploy expedite` when shipping a fix during an incident. It is logged in `#eng-changes` [2].
- **Rollback:** always allowed, at any time, without approval [1][2].

**Other constraints that still apply**
- Deploys run Monday to Thursday, 09:00–16:00 Pacific. Friday deploys need approval from the on-call engineering manager [2].

rows.answer:
**No, don't run `nwctl scale ingest` on us-west.** Hydrant, the automatic gateway scaler, has managed us-west's replica count since October 15. A manual change will be reverted within 2 minutes [2][6]. The runbook copy I found still lists the manual step [1], but the Hydrant launch notes say it replaces that step [2].

**What to do instead**

1. **Confirm the cell and check TLS errors first.** The runbook's first steps still apply: check which cell is affected and look at gateway TLS handshake errors [1][2]. The August us-east outage (INC-2291) was a TLS handshake failure on the gateways, with broker logs showing no errors [3].
2. **Check whether Hydrant is already scaling.** Hydrant scales up when average gateway CPU stays above 65% for 3 minutes, adding 25% of current replicas (at least 2) per step [2]. At 80%+ CPU, replicas should be climbing. If they aren't, the cause is probably one of the two cases below.
   - **Ceiling reached:** us-west's range is 10 to 48 replicas [6]. If the cell sits at its ceiling for 10 minutes, Hydrant pages the Data Plane primary on-call, because a ceiling hit usually means a gateway problem, not real traffic [2].
   - **Controller down:** if the Hydrant controller is down, it pages the Platform primary. Gateways keep their last replica count in that case [2].
3. **Pin the count only if you need to.** For example, while debugging a bad gateway build, use:
   `nwctl hydrant hold --cell us-west --replicas <n> --ttl 2h`
   A hold lasts at most 4 hours, then Hydrant takes over again. It is a standard change and needs no approval. Release it early with `nwctl hydrant release --cell us-west` [2].
4. **Don't raise the ceiling mid-incident.** Changing a cell's floor or ceiling is a normal change that needs sign-off from PLAT's change approver [2][6].
5. **Declare if customers are affected.** Use `/incident declare` in Slack. A full ingest outage for a cell is SEV-1, and a partial outage or degraded performance affecting many customers is SEV-2 [1].

I can't see live metrics, so I can't tell you the current us-west replica count or whether the ceiling has been reached. Check the Hydrant state for us-west before taking any action.

**The full cutover to the new payment provider is scheduled for January 19, 2027.** The most recent update I found (October 26, 2026) gives that date, and it falls after the holiday freeze and after January invoices go out [1].

**Current state**
- Dual-running has been live since October 19. About 5% of Growth workspaces have card payments collected through the new provider, and Ledger writes to both providers. Reconciliation shows no mismatches so far [1].
- The migration is codenamed Undertow. It covers moving card collection and Ledger's customer tokens to the new provider [3].

**Milestones and dependencies**
- **November 12, 2026:** Customer token migration rehearsal #2. It was moved from October 30 because that date falls in the month-end billing freeze. Arjun Mehta runs it, and Noor Haddad will check what customers would see in billing emails [1].

- Lantern's beta is now February 2027 [2][3]. Lantern plan changes are blocked on Undertow [1].

The firehose is the **`ingest-gateway`** service, and it handles **Restricted** data, owned by the **Data Plane (DP)** team.

- **Data class:** The service catalog lists `ingest-gateway` as Restricted. It accepts events from customer SDKs and the HTTP API, authenticates them, and writes them to Kafka. It keeps only in-flight event payloads, nothing beyond the Kafka hot buffer [1]. The information security policy defines Restricted data as customer event payloads, credentials, and encryption keys. That data never leaves production and never goes into tickets or Slack [6].
- **Owner:** DP owns `ingest-gateway` [1]. The Data Plane team's engineering manager and change approver is Priya Raman, with Lin Zhou as delegate, and the team's Slack channel is `#team-dataplane` [3].
- **Naming:** "The firehose" is an informal Slack and incident-channel name for `ingest-gateway`. Use the real service name in runbooks, postmortems, and tickets [2].

For day-to-day operations, the on-call runbook says the Data Plane team covers ingest gateways, pipeline runners, and connectors, on a one-week rotation with a primary and a secondary [4]. Hydrant, the gateway autoscaler, is a separate PLAT-owned service. When a cell sits at its replica ceiling for 10 minutes, it pages the Data Plane primary on-call [7]. I did not find a more specific day-to-day maintainer for the firehose beyond the team-level ownership.

rows.answer:
**Short answer: 365 days by default.** Archived events in the attic are deleted once they pass that retention period. This is the current standard, which took effect September 15, 2026 and replaced the earlier 400-day default [2][1].

**What "the attic" is**

"The attic" is an informal name for Driftwood, the long-term event archive. Older documents call it the cold store [3]. Driftwood is a Platform (PLAT)-owned object archive that stores archived event payloads, partitioned by workspace and day [5].

**How deletion works**

- Object-storage lifecycle rules on the Driftwood buckets delete archived objects once they pass the retention period for their workspace [2].
- Per-workspace overrides are stored as bucket tags [2].
- Changing those lifecycle rules is a normal change under the production change approval policy [2][6].

**Overrides and exceptions**

- Enterprise customers can contract for longer archive retention, up to 730 days, with approval from the security team [2].
- The v1 standard also let Enterprise customers contract for a shorter archive period [1]. The v2 standard doesn't mention shorter periods, so I can't confirm from the knowledge base whether that option still exists.
- A pricing policy says custom retention beyond 400 days needs security team approval [4]. That figure matches the superseded v1 default, so this policy appears out of date. The v2 standard is the one to follow [2].

**Related deletion timelines**

- Verified deletion requests, such as GDPR erasure, are completed in all live systems within 14 days. This is down from 30 days in v1 [2][1].
- When a workspace is closed, its event data in Driftwood is deleted within 14 days [2].
- Backups age out on their own 35-day schedule [2].

**Gap**

The sources don't say whether the 365-day clock starts at ingestion or at archiving. They only say objects are deleted once they pass the retention period for their workspace [2]. The Security team reviews the standard every six months, and the next review is due March 2027 [2].

rows.answer:
**Answer:** For a P2 ticket from an Enterprise customer with Premium Support, the first-response target is **1 hour**, and you must send updates **every 2 hours**. Coverage is 24/7 [1].

The current targets are in the SLA tiers document effective August 1, 2026. Tickets opened on or after that date use these targets [1].

**Key details**
- **Priority:** P2 means a production pipeline is degraded (late or partially failing) with no reasonable workaround [1].
- **Coverage:** P2 is 24/7 for this tier, so business hours don't affect the clock [1].
- **Premium Support:** It is sold only with Enterprise and includes a named TAM and the response targets above [1]. For P1 tickets, the TAM joins the call [1]. The TAM's role for P2 isn't specified.

**How this compares to other Enterprise levels**
- Enterprise without Premium Support, P2: first response in 2 hours, updates every 4 hours, 24/7 [1].
- The 2026 edition lowered Enterprise P2 first response from 4 hours to 2 hours [1]. The Premium Support row (1 hour, every 2 hours) is the tighter target [1].

**Things to watch**
- **Superseded numbers:** The 2025 edition listed Enterprise P2 at 4 hours with updates every 8 hours [2]. It no longer applies to tickets opened on or after August 1, 2026 [1].
- **Service credits:** Credits for missed first responses apply only to Enterprise P1 tickets, at 5% of the month's fee per miss, capped at 25% per month [1]. The 2025 edition said there were no credits for missed response targets [2]. Under the 2026 edition, a missed P2 first response has no credit, but the 2025 edition said missed Enterprise P1 and P2 first responses were reviewed weekly by Support Operations [2]. I didn't find a 2026 version of that review rule.
- **Priority changes:** The 2025 edition says Support may change a ticket's priority after triage but must tell the customer why [2]. I didn't find this rule in the 2026 edition.
- **Where tickets must live:** Slack Connect messages don't start an SLA clock, and tickets must be tracked in the helpdesk [2][1].
- **Helpdesk constraints:** The helpdesk vendor, Hollowpine, is operating under a security exception because its DPA is unsigned [7]. AI reply suggestions must stay disabled until the DPA is signed [7]. Agents must not ask customers to paste event payloads, credentials, or encryption keys into tickets [7][1].

I found no exception in the Support or Vendors documents that changes the P2 first-response or update timelines for Enterprise customers with Premium Support.

The most ingest gateways Hydrant will run in the us-east-2 cell is **40 replicas**.

The us-east-2 region hosts the `us-central` cell, located in Ohio [2]. Its Hydrant gateway floor is 8 and its ceiling is 40 [2]. Hydrant scales gateway replicas between that cell's floor and ceiling [1].

I found no general, cross-cell maximum that would override this, so 40 is the limit that applies. Don't confuse this cell with `us-east`, which is in us-east-1 and has a ceiling of 64 [2].

A few caveats:
- The 40 figure comes from the production cell inventory, last updated October 23, 2026 [2]. Floors and ceilings live in the PLAT infrastructure repo, which I couldn't check, so confirm there if the number matters for a decision.
- Changing the ceiling is a normal change that needs sign-off from PLAT's change approver [1][2].
- If a cell sits at its ceiling for 10 minutes, Hydrant pages the Data Plane primary on-call [1].
- Operators can pin a replica count with `nwctl hydrant hold`, but holds last at most 4 hours [1]. I found no source confirming whether a hold can exceed the ceiling.

For a Growth workspace, the legacy `POST /v1/track` endpoint is limited to **500 requests per second** [1]. Limits are applied per workspace, not per API key, so all keys in one workspace share that budget [1].

Other details for this endpoint:

- **Batch size:** each request accepts up to 100 events [1].
- **Bursts:** short bursts up to 2x the limit are allowed for 10 seconds [1].
- **Over the limit:** the API returns HTTP 429 with a `Retry-After` header. The SDKs honour it automatically [1].
- **No increases:** `/v1/track` keeps its lower limits until it is switched off, and Northwind says it will not raise them for anyone [1].

**Deprecation:** the endpoint stops accepting events on April 30, 2027 [1][2]. SDKs released after March 2025 already use `/v2/events` [1][2]. For comparison, Growth gets 2,000 req/s on `POST /v2/events` and 50 req/s on `POST /v2/events/batch` [1].

The rate-limit table is from the Engineering document "Northwind Pipelines API rate limits by plan," last updated October 21, 2026 [1]. I did not find a separate migration guide in the knowledge base.

**An account executive can approve 12% off a Growth deal.** Under the current rules, that discount needs no deal desk review and no manager sign-off.

The October 1, 2026 sales desk memo sets the approval matrix for quotes issued on or after that date. For Growth deals, a discount over 10% and up to 15% is approved by an account executive, with no deal desk review and a target turnaround of one business day [2].

**Why the older table doesn't apply:** The original Pricing and discount policy listed 10–20% as regional sales director territory [1]. The later memo replaces that table, and the rest of the policy stays in force [2]. Since today is October 31, 2026, the memo governs.

**Related rules that affect this request:**
- **Deal desk:** Any discount above 15% goes to the deal desk (run by Priscilla Okoye in sales operations) before it reaches the approver [2]. Growth discounts above 15% go to a regional sales director, then higher as the discount grows [2]. If the customer's ask moves above 15%, the request changes approver.
- **Recording approval:** The approver must record the decision in the CRM. Email and Slack approvals don't count [2].
- **Validity:** Approvals last 30 days. A quote that changes by more than 2 percentage points needs fresh approval [2].
- **Multi-year extras:** Multi-year deals can add 5% per committed year, capped at 10%. That extra doesn't count toward the approval thresholds [1][2].
- **Non-profit and education:** These customers get 50% off Growth automatically, with no approval needed [1][2].

**Open question:** The sources don't say whether a negotiated 12% can be combined with the 15% discount for annual prepayment on Growth [1][2]. Check with sales operations or the CRO before quoting both together.

**Answer: every 3 business days.** For a Growth customer's P3 ticket, send a customer update at least every 3 business days, during business hours [2].

The current schedule is the August 1, 2026 edition, which applies to tickets opened on or after that date [2]. The 2025 edition said "as needed" for Growth P3 and P4 [1], so that older guidance no longer applies.

**Growth P3 targets (2026 edition)** [2]:
- **First response:** 2 business days
- **Update cadence:** every 3 business days
- **Coverage:** business hours, which are 08:00–18:00 Monday to Friday in the customer's support region (US Pacific, US Eastern, or UK), excluding that region's public holidays [2]

**What P3 means:** a bug or question with a workaround available [2].

**Other Growth cadences, for comparison** [2]:

| Priority | Update cadence |
|---|---|
| P1 | Every 4 hours (24/7) |
| P2 | Daily (business hours) |
| P3 | Every 3 business days (business hours) |
| P4 | As needed (business hours) |

**Tier and exceptions:**
- Growth is a plan priced at $1,200 per month with 100 million included events [3]. The support documents I found don't define Growth entitlements beyond this table.
- Premium Support, with a named TAM and a 4-hour P3 response, is only sold with Enterprise and cannot be added to Growth [2].
- I found no Growth-specific exception to the P3 cadence.
- I did not find guidance on how to handle a P3 that Support reclassifies to a different priority. If that happens, the cadence for the new priority applies.

rows.answer:
**Short answer: an Enterprise workspace can force a reference-table snapshot rebuild once every 2 minutes through the API.** The limit is set by `POST /v2/reference-tables/{id}/refresh` [1].

## Enterprise limit

- **Rate:** 1 per 2 minutes, per workspace [1].
- **Scope:** Limits are per workspace, not per API key, so ten keys in one workspace share one budget [1].
- **Over the limit:** The API returns HTTP 429 with a `Retry-After` header. Rejected requests don't count against the monthly event quota [1].
- **Burst:** The general rule allows short bursts of up to 2x the limit for 10 seconds [1]. The page doesn't say whether that applies to this endpoint, so don't rely on it.

## How it differs by plan

| Plan | Forced snapshot rebuild limit |
|---|---|
| Starter | Not available (HTTP 403, not 429) [1] |
| Growth | 1 per 10 minutes [1] |
| Enterprise | 1 per 2 minutes [1] |

- The Enterprise option to raise limits by contract (up to 3x) covers only `/v2/events` and `/v2/events/batch`, not the refresh endpoint [1].
- Temporary raises for a one-off backfill (up to 72 hours) can be granted by the DP on-call primary on any plan that has the endpoint [1]. The page doesn't say whether this applies to refresh calls, and it's written for backfills.

## Why it's limited

A forced refresh discards the runner's snapshot and rebuilds it with a full table scan, which is expensive on large tables. Snapshots are normally kept current with change data capture, so most customers never need to force one [1].

## Other rebuild behavior

- **Automatic rebuilds:** Runners rebuild from scratch on restart or when CDC lag exceeds 10 minutes [2][3]. The docs I found don't say whether these automatic rebuilds count against the API limit.
- **Proposed change:** RFC-031 proposes writing a compacted snapshot every 15 minutes and restoring from it on restart, with a target restore time under 90 seconds for a 50M-row table [2]. This is a proposal, not shipped behavior. Its security review was still pending when the RFC was written [2].
- **Feature status:** Enrich (the feature these snapshots serve) is in private beta as of the October 1, 2026 changelog [4]. GA is targeted for January 2027 [3]. Your workspace may not have this endpoint yet.

## Other questions

- **Cooldowns, quotas or concurrency limits in Support or Engineering docs:** The only limit I found is the per-workspace 2-minute interval above [1]. The Support SLA pages cover response times, not API limits [5][6].
- **Vendor documents:** None in the Vendors collection governs snapshot rebuild behavior. The vendor registers I found cover Hollowpine (support ticketing), Parcelwise (email) and Saltmarsh (product analytics), and none of them mention reference tables or snapshots [7][8][9].
- **Snapshot retention (related):** Reference-table snapshots are kept in runner local state or Driftwood, and deleted 7 days after they are replaced [10].

Sources: [1] Northwind Pipelines API rate limits by plan (Engineering, updated Oct 21, 2026); [2] RFC-031 (Engineering); [3] Streaming joins product spec (Engineering); [4] Pipelines changelog, Oct 2026 (Engineering); [5] Support SLA tiers, Aug 2026 (Support); [6] Support SLA tiers, 2025 edition (Support); [7] Hollowpine vendor register (Vendors); [8] Parcelwise vendor register (Vendors); [9] Saltmarsh vendor register (Vendors); [10] Customer data retention standard v2 (Company).

rows.answer:
The knowledge base doesn't document a rate limit for `/v2/destinations`, so I can't give you a Growth number for it.

**What I checked**
- The internal rate limit page, which says it is the source of truth for the public docs, lists limits for event ingest, pipelines, usage, reference tables, audit log export and SCIM. It has no `/v2/destinations` row [1].
- Searches for "destinations" across Engineering and Support returned no endpoint-specific limit.
- The September–October 2026 changelog and the October 2026 incident log mention no rate limit change for destinations [4][8].

**Related Growth limits (not for destinations)**
The closest documented Growth limits are for the management-style endpoints [1]:
- `GET /v2/pipelines`: 50 req/s
- `POST /v2/pipelines/{id}/runs`: 10 req/s
- `GET /v2/usage`: 10 req/s

Limits are per workspace, not per API key, and the API returns HTTP 429 with a `Retry-After` header when a limit is exceeded. Short bursts up to 2x the limit are allowed for 10 seconds [1].

**Growth overrides**
Growth limits are fixed by contract. Customers who need more are directed to talk to sales about Enterprise. Temporary raises of up to 72 hours for one-off backfills can be granted by the DP on-call primary [1].

**Next step**
Ask the team that owns the endpoint for the authoritative number. The rate limit page says the management API is owned by Workspace Experience (WX) [1]. I haven't confirmed that `/v2/destinations` falls under it, so the owner should also confirm that.

**INC-2351 has no documented root cause yet.** The postmortem is still under review, so I can't tell you what caused it or what follow-up actions came out of it.

**What is recorded about the incident**
- INC-2351 was a SEV-2 on October 14. Snowflake destinations failed to load for 63 workspaces in the us-east and us-west cells. The incident lasted 1h 50m, and Harriet Vance was incident commander [1].

**Status of the postmortem**
- The incident log lists INC-2351 as "In review." The postmortem draft was circulated on October 21 and is due for review at the reliability meeting on November 5. The root cause and action items will be added to the log once the postmortem is accepted [1].
- The log also asks that no one speculate about the cause in customer conversations [1].

**Follow-ups and escalations**
- I found no action items, owners, or due dates for INC-2351 in the knowledge base.
- I found no record of INC-2351 being escalated to Leadership or Vendors. My searches of the Engineering collection and the wider Northwind Labs knowledge base returned nothing on this.

**Don't confuse it with other incidents**
- The Snowflake-related note in the log for INC-2264 concerns one workspace whose credentials were rotated. It is a different, SEV-3 incident [1].
- The INC-2340 and INC-2291 write-ups in the knowledge base are complete, but they are separate incidents. Their root causes and follow-ups don't apply to INC-2351 [1][3][5].

To get an answer, check the reliability meeting outcome on November 5 or ask Harriet Vance, the incident commander, for the accepted postmortem.

rows.answer:
**Short answer:** Yes, but only connection logs, and only for 30 days. Coriander does not record visits. I found no retention period for video visit logs in the Clinical Operations or People And Policy documents.

**What Coriander keeps**
- Coriander's connection logs include IP address, room ID and timestamps. It keeps them for 30 days, for troubleshooting [7].
- Visit recordings are disabled at the account level, and Coriander cannot turn them on [7]. The platform requirements say recordings are never made [2], and the October steering committee decided recordings stay off with no exceptions, including for training [1].
- Media is encrypted in transit end to end between participants and Coriander's media servers [7]. The vendor record lists the PHI as live encrypted audio and video streams, room metadata and display names, with no recordings [7].

**Coriander is not yet the platform for your current visits**
- Your current telehealth video visits run on Larkspur. Its PHI entry is visit metadata and in-call audio and video, which are not recorded [3].
- Coriander is the SDK under Juniper, the replacement platform, which is still in development [3]. The steering committee set the Juniper pilot for January 12, 2027 at three clinics, with network-wide rollout on March 2, 2027 and Larkspur shutting down on March 31, 2027 [1].
- So the 30-day log retention describes Coriander's handling once Juniper is live. I found nothing in the knowledge base about what logs Larkspur keeps or for how long.

**Retention requirements in policy**
- The Clinical Operations and People And Policy documents I searched do not set a retention or deletion period for video visit logs. The HIPAA privacy policy excerpt I found covers audits and training only [4].
- The retention language the Privacy Officer owes by November 6, 2026 is for the Tallgrass survey BAA, not video logs [9].

**Gaps to check**
- The 30-day figure comes from Halcyon's vendor record for Coriander [7]. I did not find the BAA or contract text itself, so confirm the figure there before relying on it.
- Ask the Privacy Officer or Virtual Care (Dana Okafor, the Coriander record owner [7]) whether Larkspur keeps any logs and what its retention period is.

**Short answer:** The AI scribe (Quillon Ambient) deletes visit audio within 7 days after the clinician signs the note [1].

**Supporting detail**

- **Deletion timing:** The vendor record states "Deleted within 7 days after the note is signed" [1]. The BAA was executed July 30, 2026, and the security risk assessment was completed in July 2026 [1].
- **Scope:** Quillon is in a 12-month pilot at Riverside and Elm Park, with 60 clinicians starting August 17, 2026 [1]. Patients must give verbal consent at the start of every visit, and the clinician must review and sign every note [2].

**Audio vs. transcripts and notes**

The knowledge base only sets a deletion period for audio. The vendor record lists visit audio, transcripts, draft notes, and patient name and date of birth as PHI the vendor handles, but gives no separate retention period for transcripts or draft notes [1]. The systems inventory lists Quillon as holding "visit audio, draft notes" [4]. The signed note itself goes into Meridian EHR, which is the clinical record [1][4]. I did not find a stated deletion period for transcripts or draft notes held by Quillon, so that question remains open.

**Contract and exceptions**

- **Contract terms:** The vendor record says model training on Halcyon data is prohibited by the BAA [1]. I did not find the BAA text or any deletion clause beyond the 7-day summary, so the 7-day figure comes from Halcyon's internal summary, not the contract itself.
- **Legal holds:** I found no legal-hold or preservation exception for Quillon audio in the knowledge base.
- **Quality review:** The pilot includes a note accuracy audit of 30 notes per clinician, reviewed by Clinical Informatics [1]. The source doesn't say whether this review uses audio, so I can't confirm whether it extends audio retention.
- **Recording opt-outs:** Clinicians can turn off recording in the Quillon app if a patient declines [1]. The Juniper steering committee also decided that recordings stay off, with no exceptions, including for training [3]. That decision concerns the Juniper telehealth platform, not Quillon.

If you need to confirm the period for a compliance or legal purpose, check the executed Quillon BAA with the Privacy Officer (Margaret Holloway) or the HIPAA Security Officer (Ahmed Siddiqui), since the knowledge base doesn't include the contract text.

**Short answer:** Access is suspended automatically once your HIPAA training is more than 14 days overdue [1]. Halcyon's annual deadline is January 31 [1], so if you missed the most recent one, you are already past the 14-day threshold and may already be locked out.

**The rules**

- Every workforce member must complete HIPAA training during onboarding and annually by January 31 [1].
- Clinical system access is suspended automatically if training is overdue by more than 14 days [1].
- Applied to a January 31 deadline, that means suspension would begin in mid-February. This is my calculation from the policy, not a stated date.

**What I could not find**

- The knowledge base does not describe how access is restored after you finish overdue training. I found no reinstatement steps, turnaround time, or approver.
- I also could not confirm your individual due date. If your assignment differs from the January 31 default, check your training record.

**What to do now**

1. Complete the HIPAA training as soon as possible.
2. If you are locked out, open a ticket with the IT Service Desk (extension 4357, or the Service Desk tile on the intranet) [7]. The knowledge base says to open a ticket for every problem [7]. I did not find a training-specific route, so the Service Desk is the best starting point.
3. If you have questions about your training status or the policy, contact the Privacy Officer at privacy@halcyon.example [1].

rows.answer:
**Direct answer:** The patient should be handed off to the medical assistant within 10 minutes of check-in. This is step 4 of the check-in process in Halcyon's Patient intake procedure, which applies to all clinics and the telehealth front desk [1].

**Related timing targets**

- **Door-to-room:** Halcyon's target is under 15 minutes for 90% of visits [1]. This is a broader measure than the 10-minute handoff, which covers only the check-in step.
- **Interpreters:** Video interpreters should be available within 2 minutes, in more than 200 languages [1].
- **Staffing context:** The current staffing standard (effective September 1, 2026) was revised because medium and large clinics were missing the door-to-room target on most afternoons [2].

**Variations by visit type or location**

- I found no exceptions to the 10-minute handoff for visit type, clinic, or session. The intake procedure applies uniformly, including to the telehealth front desk [1].
- Saturday and Sunday sessions follow the same procedure, but they have their own staffing minimums [2]. The directory lists reduced hours for those sessions [6].
- Don't confuse the 10-minute handoff with the 10-minute late-arrival rule. A patient who arrives more than 10 minutes after their appointment time may be offered another slot that day or be rescheduled [3]. That rule governs appointment timing, not the handoff.

**Staffing and vendor requirements**

- The clinic staffing standard sets minimum staff by clinic size, such as medical assistants per clinician, RNs, and front desk staff. It does not set a handoff or wait-time requirement [2].

**No, don't throw the vaccines out.** Halcyon's policy says to quarantine the stock, not discard it, until the clinical pharmacist has checked it with the manufacturers [1].

**What to do now**

1. **Don't discard anything.** Label the affected stock "Do not use" and move it to a working refrigerated unit. Record the reading, the time, and how long the fridge has been out of range [1].
2. **Call the clinical pharmacist within 1 hour.** The pharmacist checks with the manufacturers whether the stock can still be used [1].
3. **File a SafeReport.** Use a Level 4 near miss if no vaccine from the affected stock was given. If a patient received affected vaccine, the level is higher [1]. The sentinel and adverse event policy says that when you're unsure, report at the higher level, and Quality & Patient Safety will reclassify if needed [3].
4. **Don't give any vaccine from the affected stock** until the clinical pharmacist releases it in writing [1].

Vaccine fridges must stay between 2 °C and 8 °C, so 10 °C is out of range [1].

**What the knowledge base doesn't cover**

- **Time limits:** None of the sources say how long vaccines can tolerate a temperature excursion, so I can't tell you whether this stock is likely still usable. That decision belongs to the pharmacist.
- **Vendor guidance:** I found no manufacturer or vendor excursion or replacement procedures in the Vendors collection. The only route in the documents is the pharmacist's check with manufacturers [1].
- **Weekend coverage:** Today is Saturday. The sources don't say how to reach the clinical pharmacist on weekends or who covers if they can't be reached. Your clinic manager is the person to escalate to, but no source confirms that for vaccine excursions.

**Call the Halcyon answering service at 555-0144 and choose option 2.** The service pages the on-call medical director, and if there is no callback within 10 minutes, it pages the backup [1]. For the week of October 26 to November 2, the on-call medical director is Dr. Priya Natarajan, with Dr. Samuel Achterberg as backup [1]. The shift changes Monday at 08:00 Eastern, when Dr. Helen Mwangi takes over (backup Dr. Luis Carvalho) [1].

**Don't text personal mobile numbers.** Pages through the answering service are logged and timed, which the chart documentation needs [1].

## Backup path

- The answering service pages the backup automatically if the on-call director doesn't call back within 10 minutes [1].
- I found no documented step beyond the backup. If neither responds, the sources don't say what to do next.

## When to contact the on-call medical director

The on-call director is the senior physician for the whole network, outside each clinic's normal supervision. They handle critical lab results when the ordering clinician can't be reached, sentinel event notifications, emergency clinical system changes, transfers, unexpected closures, and any clinical question a supervising physician can't resolve [1].

Specific triggers in the policies:

- **Emergencies come first.** For chest pain with shortness of breath, stroke signs, SpO2 below 90% on room air, symptomatic BP above 180 or below 90, or active suicidal ideation with a plan, call 911 and notify the on-site clinician immediately [2]. For telehealth patients with red-flag symptoms, keep the video call open, confirm the patient's location, and call 911 on a separate line [2].
- **Critical lab results.** Results must reach the ordering clinician within 60 minutes. If that clinician can't be reached within 30 minutes, the result goes to the on-call medical director [2].
- **Supervising physician within 30 minutes.** Fever above 39.4 °C in an adult (or any fever in an infant under 3 months), new confusion in a patient over 65, a critical value called in by the reference lab, or glucose above 400 or below 60 mg/dL [2]. The protocol doesn't name the on-call director for these, so start with the supervising physician.
- **Sentinel events.** The charge nurse notifies the on-call medical director within 1 hour. Report any event in SafeReport as well [3].

I found no guidance on which after-hours questions can wait until business hours. For anything urgent that you can't resolve with the supervising physician, the rota's stated scope is the on-call director's remit [1].

## Expectations for the on-call director

The director must answer pages within 10 minutes, day or night, and stay within 45 minutes of a Halcyon clinic during the shift [1]. Note that the rota doc is titled "November 2026" but covers the week starting October 26 [1].

rows.answer:
**Short answer:** Halcyon's standard is **10 business days** for a patient copy that isn't available instantly in the portal. HIPAA allows up to **30 calendar days**, which is the outer legal limit [1].

**Deadlines**

- **Halcyon standard:** 10 business days for electronic (secure email or encrypted USB) or paper copies, which cost a $6.50 flat fee [1].
- **HIPAA outer limit:** 30 calendar days [1].
- **Portal downloads:** immediate and free. Most of the record, including visit notes, results and immunizations, can be downloaded there [1].

If the request came in today (Saturday, October 31), counting 10 business days from Monday, November 2 puts the target around November 13. That assumes no holidays, and the knowledge base doesn't say whether Halcyon observes Veterans Day (November 11). The 30-day HIPAA limit would fall around November 30. Use the date the request was actually received, not the date you read about it.

**Handling the request**

- Point the patient to the portal first, since most of the record is available there at no charge [1].
- Don't delay the request because of an unpaid balance [1].
- Fees are waived for patients in the sliding-fee program [1].
- Sensitive records with extra legal protection, such as substance use treatment records, are released only after the Privacy Officer reviews the request. The knowledge base doesn't give a timeline for that review, so build extra time in and check with the Privacy Officer [1].
- Requests from law enforcement or under subpoena go to the Privacy Officer, not HIM staff [1].

**Who owns it**

- Health Information Management (HIM) owns patient record requests. The HIM supervisor is Joanna Kowalczyk [1].
- Every request is logged in the HIM request queue in Meridian EHR, which is where the deadline should be tracked [1].
- HIM can be reached through the intranet or at him@halcyon.example [1].

**Vendor exceptions**

I found no vendor agreement or exception that changes the turnaround for releasing patient records. The vendor support matrix covers system support response times, not record release [6]. The only other turnaround rules I found are for other types of requests, such as sending records to another treating provider (3 business days) or to an attorney or insurer (15 business days) [1].

**Within 72 hours.** A medication error that needed treatment is a Level 2 event (adverse event with harm). Under Halcyon's Sentinel and adverse event reporting policy, every Level 1 and Level 2 event gets a root cause analysis, and QPS charters the RCA team within 72 hours [1].

**Related timing and requirements**

- **Immediate:** Make the patient safe, then tell the charge nurse on shift (or the clinic manager if there is no charge nurse) [1].
- **Within 24 hours:** Anyone involved or who witnessed the event files a SafeReport, and the attending clinician discloses the event to the patient or family [1].
- **RCA completion:** The RCA must be finished within 45 calendar days of the event becoming known [1].
- **Review:** Completed RCAs and their action plans go to the Patient Safety Committee, chaired by the CMO, Dr. Kenji Watanabe [1].

**Exceptions and severity differences**

- The policy does not give an exception for medication errors. Level 1 (sentinel) and Level 2 events both require an RCA on the same 72-hour charter timeline [1]. The policy does not state a different timeline for Level 1 events.
- Level 3 (error reached the patient, no harm) and Level 4 (near miss) events are not listed as requiring an RCA [1].
- If you are unsure of the level, report at the higher level. QPS can reclassify later [1].
- Software-caused events follow the same policy, with fixes going through clinical systems change control [1].

**Gaps to be aware of**

- The policy says the 72-hour clock runs for charter, but it does not say exactly when that clock starts. The 45-day completion clock starts when the event becomes known [1].
- I did not find a separate medication-error policy in the knowledge base. The answer above comes from the sentinel and adverse event policy, which is the document that defines Level 2 events and the RCA requirement.

**Short answer:** Keep trying the ordering clinician for up to 30 minutes. If you still can't reach them, send the result to the on-call medical director. For Wednesday, November 18, that is Dr. Luis Carvalho, with Dr. Ingrid Solberg as backup. The policy sets a 60-minute target for the result to reach the ordering clinician [1].

**The timeline**

- **Target:** a critical result must reach the ordering clinician within 60 minutes [1].
- **At 30 minutes:** if the ordering clinician can't be reached, the result goes to the medical director on call [1].
- **How to page:** call the Halcyon answering service at 555-0144 and choose option 2. The service pages the on-call medical director, and if there is no callback within 10 minutes, it pages the backup. Don't text physicians' personal mobile numbers [2].

The on-call shift runs Monday 08:00 to the following Monday 08:00 Eastern. Wednesday, November 18 falls in the week of November 16 to November 23 [2]:

| Role | Name |
|---|---|
| On-call medical director | Dr. Luis Carvalho [2] |
| Backup | Dr. Ingrid Solberg [2] |

The rota lists no swaps for that week. The only November swap is Thanksgiving [2].

- Record the time and the person notified in the chart for every critical result notification [1].
- Record the escalation in the encounter note: the time, who was notified, and the outcome [1].
- Pages through the answering service are logged and timed, which is what the chart documentation relies on [2].

I found no weekday- or after-hours-specific requirements for critical result escalation. The on-call medical director answers pages day or night [2]. If the result is still open at the Monday 08:00 handover, pending critical results are covered in that handover [2].

**Gaps in the policy**

- The sources don't say exactly when the 30-minute window starts. I'd assume it starts at your first attempt to reach the ordering clinician, but confirm this with your clinic manager or Clinical Operations.
- The protocol doesn't say whether you should keep calling the ordering clinician after you escalate to the medical director.

The formulary already gives the key constraint: the shingles vaccine is Tier 2, so Elmhurst may not stock it. I'll check which hub serves Elmhurst, the screening rules, and vendor restrictions.**No, not at Elmhurst today.** Elmhurst doesn't stock the shingles vaccine, and it can't be given there on a same-day basis.

- The recombinant zoster vaccine (RZV, Shingrix) is Tier 2, which means it's stocked at hub clinics only [5]. Elmhurst is not a hub [3].
- Elmhurst has to request a transfer from its nearest hub. Transfers arrive within 2 business days [5].
- Today is Saturday. If the request goes in today, the earliest arrival would be around Tuesday, November 3, counting Monday and Tuesday as the two business days. That is my estimate, not something the documents state.

## What the patient needs

- **Eligibility:** RZV is for ages 50 and over. It's a 2-dose series, with the second dose 2–6 months after the first [5].
- **Price:** $205 per dose for self-pay patients. The 20% prompt-pay discount doesn't apply to vaccines. Sliding-fee patients get the program discount [5].
- **Who can give it:** an RN or a clinician. Medical assistants can't give RZV [5].

## Same-day options

- **Send the patient to a hub.** Northgate (Saturday 08:00–14:00) and Harbor Point (Saturday 08:00–16:00) are hub clinics open today [3]. Riverside is also a hub but closes at 12:00 on Saturdays [3]. I couldn't confirm which hub is nearest to Elmhurst, so check the directory or the clinical pharmacist.
- **Check Elmhurst's Saturday coverage.** Elmhurst's Saturday hours are 09:00–12:00 [3]. The current staffing standard requires at least one physician or NP and one RN on site for any Saturday session [9]. I couldn't find the actual rota for today.

## Screening and clinical requirements

The knowledge base has no RZV-specific contraindication or screening checklist. It only gives the age rule and dosing interval above. The standard intake steps (vitals, medication reconciliation, allergies, and the PHQ-2 screen) apply to every visit [1]. Please check the clinical guidance for anything else before administering.

## Vendors and distribution

I found no vaccine supplier or wholesaler contract in the knowledge base, so I can't say whether any contract restricts where RZV can be distributed. The only vendor record I found is the Quillon Ambient AI scribe agreement, which isn't relevant here [4]. Tier 3 items are ordered from the wholesaler for a named patient, with a 5-business-day lead time [5].

## Source conflict to note

The 2025 staffing standard said Saturday sessions didn't need an RN [7]. The September 2026 standard replaces it and requires one [9], so the 2026 version should be used.

**Answer: Riverbend should be scheduled at 1.5 medical assistants per clinician.** Under the current standard, Riverbend is in the Medium band, which sets the ratio at 1.5 [1][3].

**Why Riverbend is Medium**
- The current standard is the clinic staffing standard effective September 1, 2026. It was approved August 10, 2026 by Rosa Delgado and Marisol Vance, and it replaces the 2025 standard [1].
- Bands are set by "Avg visits per day" in the clinic directory, and are reset every quarter [1].
- Riverbend averaged 46 visits per day in Q3 2026 (July–September) [3]. That falls in the Medium band of 40 to 80 visits per day [1].

**Current staffing bands (effective September 1, 2026)** [1]

| Band | Avg visits/day | MAs per clinician | Physicians/NPs (min) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Small | Under 40 | 1.0 | 1 |
| Medium | 40–80 | 1.5 | 2 |
| Large | Over 80 | 2.0 | 3 |

**Practical application**
- The standard says "MAs per clinician" means the number of medical assistants scheduled for each physician or nurse practitioner seeing patients, and to round up to the next whole person [1].
- Read literally, a single clinician at Riverbend would get 2 MAs (1.5 rounded up). With the Medium minimum of two physicians/NPs on site, that is 3 MAs in total. The source does not say explicitly whether rounding applies per clinician or to the total, so confirm with Clinical Operations if it matters for a specific schedule.
- Riverbend is closed on Saturdays and Sundays [3], so the separate weekend session ratio (1.0) does not apply.

**Exceptions and things to watch**
- I found no Riverbend-specific exception to the standard in the knowledge base.
- Riverbend's 46 visits per day is close to the 40 threshold for Small. Its band can change at the next quarterly reset if volume drops [1][3].
- Don't confuse Riverbend (RVB) with Riverside (RVS). They are different clinics about four miles apart. Riverside averaged 94 visits per day, so it is in the Large band at 2.0 MAs per clinician [3].
- The 2025 standard had a different Medium ratio (1.25) and a different band threshold (45–90). It is superseded and should not be used for current scheduling [2].

**Short answer:** Bayline must give a first response within 30 minutes of a P1 report, and the Halcyon Service Desk pages the Integration Services system steward, Owen Mbeki, for P1 issues. A stopped results feed counts as P1.

**Bayline's response time**

- Bayline's P1 first-response time is 30 minutes, and its support is a 24/7 interface desk. P2 is 2 hours and P3 is next business day [2].
- P1 covers any problem that creates a patient-safety risk, and "results not arriving" is the example given [2].
- These are first responses from a qualified engineer, not resolution times [2].
- I did not find the Bayline agreement itself, so I can't confirm the 30-minute figure against contract text. The matrix is the only source I found for it.

**Who gets paged**

- Staff open a ticket with the Halcyon IT Service Desk (extension 4357, or the intranet tile). Clinic staff should not call Bayline directly unless the Service Desk asks them to [2].
- For any P1, the Service Desk contacts Bayline and also pages the owning team's system steward [2].
- Bayline's owning team is Integration Services (INT), which runs the HL7 feed into Switchyard [2][8].
- The INT steward is Owen Mbeki [7].

**If Bayline misses the 30 minutes**

- The Service Desk escalates to Bayline's account manager and tells the INT steward [2].
- Two missed P1 responses in one quarter are reported to the HIPAA Security Officer and recorded in the vendor's annual review [2].

**If the outage also affects clinical care**

- The on-call medical director is a separate route. It is reached through the answering service at 555-0144, option 2 [1].
- That route is for clinical escalations such as critical results the ordering clinician can't be reached about, not for the feed fault itself [1][6].
- For the week that includes today (October 31), the on-call medical director is Dr. Priya Natarajan, with Dr. Samuel Achterberg as backup. That shift ends November 2 [1].

**Related context**

- After the July 2026 Bayline incident (RCA-26-07), the feed was stopped and then restored on July 24 [3].
- The root-cause analysis found that the Bayline agreement did not require advance notice of feed format changes. An amendment requiring 30 days' notice is in progress, due December 31 [3]. This concerns change notice, not outage response time.

**Answer:** On Thanksgiving Day (Thursday, November 26, 2026), the charge nurse should notify **Dr. Ingrid Solberg**, the on-call medical director, **within 1 hour**. For a 10 a.m. event, that means by 11:00 a.m.

**Who gets the call**

- The on-call medical director is the senior physician on duty for the whole network, and the charge nurse notifies them of sentinel events [2].
- The November rota normally puts Dr. Helen Mwangi on call for week 48 (November 23–30) [2].
- For Thanksgiving, Dr. Solberg covers from 08:00 Thursday, November 26 to 08:00 Friday, November 27, in place of Dr. Mwangi [2]. A 10 a.m. event falls inside that window.
- The backup is unchanged: Dr. Daniel Ortega [2].

**How to reach them**

- Call the Halcyon answering service at **555-0144** and choose **option 2** [2].
- The service pages the on-call medical director. If there is no callback within 10 minutes, it pages the backup [2].
- Don't text physicians' personal mobile numbers. Pages through the answering service are logged and timed, which the chart documentation depends on [2].

**Timeframe**

- The sentinel event policy sets the deadline at 1 hour for the charge nurse to notify the on-call medical director [1].
- The rota does not give a separate holiday timeframe, so the standard 1-hour rule applies [1][2].

**Charge nurse's other responsibilities**

- Make the patient safe and follow the clinical escalation protocol, calling 911 if needed [1].
- Coordinate the immediate response: assign who stays with the patient, who calls the family, and who secures equipment, medications, or records involved [1].
- Anyone involved or who witnessed the event files a report in SafeReport [1].
- The attending clinician discloses the event to the patient or family, with the charge nurse or medical director present [1].

**Caveat**

Swaps must be agreed by both physicians and logged with the Office of the CMO at least 72 hours ahead so the answering service can update its schedule [2]. The rota doesn't confirm that the Thanksgiving swap has been entered into the answering service. Before the holiday, it would be worth checking with the Office of the CMO that the answering service will route to Dr. Solberg.

**Short answer:** Escalate to Meridian Clinical Systems. Its contract-level P1 response time in the Halcyon vendor matrix is 15 minutes, 24/7. The matrix is an internal summary, though, and I did not find the Meridian contract itself, so confirm the figure against the signed agreement.

**What Wren is**
- Wren is the Meridian EHR upgrade to release 2027.1, which includes new order sets, a results inbox redesign, and an updated e-prescribing module [3].
- The cutover runs Saturday, February 6, 2027, starting at 22:00 Eastern, with 6 hours of planned downtime. All clinics will use paper downtime procedures [1].

**Who to escalate to**
- Meridian Clinical Systems owns the Meridian EHR, with CI as the Halcyon owning team. Support is 24/7 with a 15-minute P1 response [2].
- For any scheduled Meridian EHR upgrade, Meridian staffs a live bridge line with its own engineers for the whole cutover window, in addition to standard 24/7 support [2]. This is the most relevant channel during the cutover itself.
- Switchyard, the lab interface engine, is built in-house and has no outside vendor. The Service Desk pages the owning team directly, using the same P1–P3 priorities [2].
- If the problem is a broken lab results feed into Switchyard, Bayline Reference Laboratories' interface desk is also relevant. It is 24/7, with a 30-minute P1 response [2].

**What counts as P1**
- P1 means the system is down or unusable at one or more clinics, or any problem that creates a patient-safety risk, such as results not arriving [2].

**If Meridian misses the response time**
- The Service Desk escalates to Meridian's account manager and tells the owning team's steward.
- Two missed P1 responses in a quarter are reported to the HIPAA Security Officer and recorded in the vendor's annual review [2].

**Cutover-specific procedure**
- I did not find a cutover incident runbook in the knowledge base. The change-control policy requires written cutover runbooks to state how double-running is prevented. That requirement came from the IR-0412 reminder incident [5][4].
- Switchyard interfaces to all reference labs must be retested by January 15, 2027 [1]. The final go/no-go is at CSCAB on January 27, 2027 [1].

**Caveats**
- Today is October 31, 2026, so the Wren cutover is more than three months away. Its plan may change before February.
- The 15-minute figure comes from the vendor matrix dated October 15, 2026 [2]. I did not verify it against the Meridian contract.
- The CSCAB minutes also record a November 18, 2026 release. The content (identifier checks and QPS reporting) matches the Heron project, not Wren [1][3].

**Elmhurst (ELH) has the AED with expired pads.** The unit is AED-ELH-01, a Vantor A3. Its pads expired on September 30, 2026, while the battery runs to April 2028 [1]. The clinic manager, Patrick Oduya, is responsible for getting it fixed [1][2].

**Who is responsible**
- **Patrick Oduya, Elmhurst clinic manager.** He took over Elmhurst on September 14, 2026 [2]. The inventory says items marked "Action needed" must be closed by the site's clinic manager, who records the fix in the equipment log and tells Clinical Operations [1].
- **Clinical Operations (Rosa Delgado, Director of Clinical Operations)** owns the emergency equipment inventory and needs to be told when the fix is recorded [1][2].

**Current status**
- Replacement pads were ordered on October 9, 2026, and are due by November 6, 2026 [1].
- Until they arrive, a spare pad set borrowed from Elm Park (ELP) is in use [1]. The inventory says this set is an A3 set that was checked as compatible before it went to Elmhurst [1].
- Vantor A3 and A5 pads are different. Pads must not be borrowed between models [1].

**Points to check**
- The inventory is dated October 26, 2026, so the status may have changed since. The pads have been expired for about a month, and the replacement is due in about six days [1].
- The knowledge base doesn't say whether the expired pads have been removed from the unit or whether the borrowed set is now the only pad set in it. Confirm this with Elmhurst.

**Procedure and vendor**
- The knowledge base has no separate written procedure for replacing AED pads. The rules that apply are the monthly AED check (self-test green, pads and battery in date, spare pad set present) and the clinic manager's duty to close action items [1].
- Vantor is the AED manufacturer, and repairs fall under a Vantor service contract that takes 2–4 weeks [1]. A failed self-test means the unit is pulled the same day and replaced with a loaner from the Clinical Operations pool [1].
- The knowledge base does not name the supplier for the replacement pads, and it has no Vantor or pad-supplier contact details. Clinical Operations would need to provide those.

- The report shows only averages, so I can't tell how many individual sessions exceeded the target. A language that met its target on average could still have had slow individual connections. [1]
- The "All other languages (61)" row is a single aggregate. Individual languages in that group aren't broken out, so I can't say whether any of them missed. [1]
- Cantonese (1:51) and American Sign Language (1:58) were close to the 2-minute limit. [1]

**Next steps:** Clinical Operations plans to raise every language that missed its target at the Polyglen renewal discussion in November 2026. Four items in the emergency equipment inventory are flagged "Action needed." The inventory was compiled October 26, 2026 [1], and I found no later update in the knowledge base, so these are the latest recorded statuses as of today.

| Asset tag | Site | Issue | Required action | Due / status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| AED-ELH-01 | Elmhurst | Pads expired Sept 30, 2026 | Replacement pads ordered Oct 9; a spare pad set borrowed from Elm Park is in use meanwhile [1] | Replacement due by Nov 6, 2026 [1] |
| OXY-NBR-01 | Northbridge | 450 psi, below the 500 psi minimum [1] | Replacement cylinder requested [1] | Not stated |
| CART-HBP-01 | Harbor Point | Monthly seal check overdue; next check was due Oct 22, 2026 [1] | Complete the seal check | Overdue since Oct 22 [1] |
| AED-CDH-01 | Cedar Hollow | Failed self-test Oct 3, 2026 and is out of service [1] | Sent to Vantor for repair [1] | Not stated; Vantor repairs under the service contract take 2–4 weeks [1] |

**Notes on each item**
- **AED-ELH-01:** The borrowed spare pads are an A3 set from Elm Park's previous unit. Vantor A3 and A5 use different pads, and the set was checked as compatible before it went to Elmhurst [1].
- **CART-HBP-01:** The inventory lists the cart as in service but flags the overdue seal check [1].
- **AED-CDH-01:** Cedar Hollow's loaner, AED-LOAN-02, stays on site until the repaired unit passes a self-test [1].

**Who closes these items**
Items marked "Action needed" must be closed by the site's clinic manager, who records the fix in the equipment log and tells Clinical Operations [1]. The managers are Patrick Oduya (Elmhurst), Simone Achebe (Northbridge), Teodor Lindqvist (Harbor Point) and Mei-Ling Cho (Cedar Hollow) [2].

**Items not flagged but worth watching**
- AED-HBP-02 (Harbor Point, urgent care bay) has pads expiring Nov 30, 2026. It is in service and new pads are already on order [1].
- Several sites have next checks due Nov 1–10, 2026 [1].

**Flagging criteria**
The inventory itself sets the criteria [1]:
- **AED:** self-test indicator green, pads and battery in date, and a spare pad set present. An AED that fails its self-test is taken out of service the same day and replaced with a loaner from the Clinical Operations pool.
- **Emergency cart:** the tamper seal number must match the log. A full restock check is done every six months by the clinical pharmacist.
- **Oxygen cylinder:** replace any cylinder below 500 psi.

I did not find a separate policy or vendor document that defines these criteria.
