Four items on the in-clinic formulary are not stocked at any clinic and must be ordered for the named patient. They are Tier 3 on the formulary, which defines Tier 3 as "not stocked" [1]:

| Item | Given by | Self-pay price | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Td (0.5 mL prefilled syringe) | RN, clinician | $46 | Tdap preferred; Td only on request [1] |
| Pneumococcal conjugate PCV21 | RN, clinician | $280 | Only when the clinician specifies PCV21 [1] |
| HPV vaccine, 9-valent | RN, clinician | $295 per dose | Ages 9–45 [1] |
| Meningococcal B vaccine | RN, clinician | $190 per dose | Ages 16–23 or on specialist advice [1] |

**How to order one for a patient**

- Tier 3 items are ordered for a named patient from the wholesaler, and you should allow 5 business days [1].
- Tier 3 named-patient orders go to the clinical pharmacist, not the weekly Tier 1 order form [1].
- Anything not on the formulary cannot be given in clinic without approval from the Pharmacy and Therapeutics subcommittee [1].
- The formulary lists Dr. Farah Qureshi, PharmD, as clinical pharmacist lead [1].

**Items that are not in the zero-stock group**

- Tier 2 items (recombinant zoster vaccine, adult hepatitis B vaccine, and ceftriaxone 500 mg IM) are stocked at hub clinics only. Riverside, Northgate and Harbor Point are the hubs [1][2]. Other clinics request a transfer from the nearest hub, which arrives within 2 business days [1].

**Limits of what I could find**

- The knowledge base has no on-hand inventory counts, so I can't confirm current stock levels for any item. The tier system is the only stock classification in the sources.
- The sources don't name the wholesaler or any vaccine vendor. The Vendors collection covers billing, IT, survey and AI-scribe vendors only [6][7][8][9][10]. Brightway Medical Supply is mentioned as a clinic supplies vendor, but nothing says it supplies vaccines [6].

Four clinics count as large under the current standard: Harbor Point, Northgate, Riverside, and Elm Park. The current standard defines large as more than 80 average in-person visits per day. The test uses the "Avg visits per day" column in the clinic directory, and bands are reset every quarter [2][3].

| Clinic | Avg visits/day (Q3 2026) | Band under current standard |
|---|---|---|
| Harbor Point (HBP) | 118 | Large |
| Northgate (NGT) | 102 | Large |
| Riverside (RVS) | 94 | Large |
| Elm Park (ELP) | 85 | Large |
| Riverbend (RVB) | 46 | Medium |
| Northbridge (NBR) | 52 | Medium |
| Elmhurst (ELH) | 38 | Small |
| Cedar Hollow (CDH) | 31 | Small |

Volumes are from [3]. Band placement is my calculation from the thresholds in [2]. Elm Park is the closest case, just above the 80 cutoff.

**What a large clinic must have** [2]:
- 3 physicians or NPs on site (minimum)
- 2.0 medical assistants per clinician
- 2 RNs on site, with one designated charge nurse
- 4 front desk staff (minimum)

The charge nurse in a large clinic also coordinates the immediate response to patient safety events [2].

**Change from the 2025 standard:** The September 1, 2026 standard replaced the 2025 version, which set large at over 90 visits a day and medium at 45–90 [1][2]. Under the 2025 standard, Elm Park (85) would have been medium, so only Riverside, Northgate, and Harbor Point were large. The new thresholds move Elm Park up to large [1][2].

**Exceptions and amendments:** I found no band overrides or exceptions in the knowledge base. The Quillon Ambient AI scribe pilot runs at Riverside and Elm Park, but its record does not change staffing bands or thresholds [5]. Because bands are reset quarterly from visit volumes, the list can change. For example, Northgate and Riverside are close to the 80 line only if volumes drop sharply [3][2].

Five vendors give 24/7 coverage for P1 problems: Meridian, Coriander Media, Bayline, Polyglen, and ClearPath (for P1 only). Larkspur, Quillon, and RotaLeaf do not.

**24/7 for P1**

| Vendor | System or service | Support hours | P1 response |
|---|---|---|---|
| Meridian Clinical Systems | Meridian EHR | 24/7 | 15 minutes [1] |
| Coriander Media | Video SDK and hosted media servers | 24/7 | 20 minutes [1] |
| Bayline Reference Laboratories | HL7 results feed into Switchyard | 24/7 interface desk | 30 minutes [1] |
| Polyglen Interpreting | Interpreter operations desk | 24/7 | 10 minutes [1] |
| ClearPath Software | ClearPath PM | 24/7 for P1 only; otherwise 07:00–19:00 Eastern, Mon–Fri | 30 minutes [1] |

Notes on these:
- **Meridian:** for scheduled EHR upgrades, Meridian also staffs a live bridge line with its own engineers for the whole cutover window [1].
- **Bayline:** the 24/7 coverage is an interface desk, not general support [1].
- **Polyglen:** P1 covers an interpreter not connecting at all. Slow connections within target are tracked in the quarterly language access report instead [1]. Separately, its contract targets a video interpreter connecting within 2 minutes for the top 20 languages and within 5 minutes for others [7].
- **Coriander:** it is also the SDK under Juniper, the in-house telehealth platform that will replace Larkspur [11].

**Not 24/7**

- **Larkspur Telehealth** (current telehealth video): 07:00–21:00 Eastern, 7 days. P1 response is 1 hour [1]. Support ends when its month-to-month extension ends [1].
- **Quillon Ambient** (AI scribe pilot): 06:00–22:00 Eastern, Mon–Sat. There is no out-of-hours P1 line; clinicians document manually [1].
- **RotaLeaf** (HR and leave): 08:00–18:00 Eastern, Mon–Fri. P1 response is 4 hours [1].

**Escalation when a vendor misses P1**

If a vendor misses its P1 response time, the Service Desk escalates to the vendor's account manager and tells the owning team's steward. Two missed P1 responses in a quarter are reported to the HIPAA Security Officer and recorded in the vendor's annual review [1].

**Clinical and policy documents**

I found no Clinical Operations or People and Policy document that sets required vendor support hours for critical incidents. The on-call medical director rota covers internal clinical coverage, not vendors [6]. The clinical escalation protocol covers patient-level escalation, not vendor response [8].

**Caveat**

The P1 terms above come from the vendor support and escalation matrix, updated October 15, 2026 [1]. I did not find the underlying contract or SLA text for each vendor, so the matrix is the only source for these hours and response times. Its verification status is not shown. If you need contractual confirmation, check the signed agreements with the owning teams.

rows.answer:
**Short answer: Halcyon no longer charges a fee for a missed appointment.** The no-show fee was eliminated effective October 5, 2026, and the revised policy replaces the 2025 version in full [1]. Staff should not try to collect any no-show fees billed before that date. Any that are still unpaid are waived, and Revenue Cycle Management reverses them on patient statements [1].

**What changed**

- The 2025 policy charged a $25 fee after a patient's second no-show in a 12-month period, with exceptions for Medicaid and sliding-fee patients [2].
- A Q2 2026 review found the fees were rarely collected, fell hardest on patients just above the sliding-fee threshold, and did not measurably reduce no-show rates [1].

**What still applies under the current policy**

- **Definition of a no-show:** the patient did not arrive or join and did not cancel at least 2 hours before the appointment. The 2025 policy used 24 hours [1][2]. Replying to an appointment reminder counts as a cancellation [1].
- **Late arrivals:** for in-person visits, a patient arriving more than 10 minutes late is offered the next open slot that day or is rescheduled. For telehealth, the clinician waits 15 minutes, and the front desk calls the patient twice during that time [1].
- **Repeat no-shows:** on the third no-show in 12 months, a care coordinator calls to identify barriers and offers help such as ride vouchers, telehealth, a different time of day, or a pre-booked interpreter. Nobody is discharged for no-shows [1].
- **Reminders:** SMS reminders go out 3 days and 1 day before in-person visits, and 2 hours before telehealth visits [1].

**Clinic and vendor differences**

- I found no clinic-specific or vendor-specific no-show fee rules. The 2025 policy said it applied "consistently at every clinic" [2], and the 2026 revision applies network-wide [1].
- The scheduling system, ClearPath PM, holds appointments and balances [13], and the billing vendor, Brightwater, prints and mails patient statements [11]. I found no document showing either one still generating a no-show charge. Given the policy change, RCM should confirm that ClearPath has no active no-show fee rule and that the reversals have been applied.

**Gap:** I did not find a fee schedule that lists a no-show charge. The only fee schedules I found cover medical records and forms [5] and self-pay visit rates [4], and neither includes a missed-appointment charge.

rows.answer:
**Short answer:** Under the current policy, front desk staff must offer a later slot or rebook once a patient arrives **more than 10 minutes** after their in-person appointment time. This threshold took effect October 5, 2026 [1].

## The current rule (in-person)

- A patient more than 10 minutes late is offered the next open slot that day with any clinician, or rescheduled [1].
- The clinician may still see the patient if the schedule allows, but the policy doesn't promise this [1].
- Patients who are late because of an interpreter or accessibility issue on Halcyon's side are never rescheduled for being late [1].

The October 2026 revision replaces the 2025 policy in full. The 2025 version had a 15-minute threshold [1][2]. Anything quoting 15 minutes is out of date.

## Related rules that affect the same visit

- **No-show definition:** A missed appointment counts as a no-show only if the patient did not cancel at least 2 hours ahead. Cancelling by replying to a reminder counts [1].
- **No-show fees:** Eliminated. Unpaid no-show fees billed before October 5, 2026 are waived, and front desk staff should not try to collect them [1].
- **Telehealth (for comparison):** The clinician waits 15 minutes after the start time, and the telehealth front desk calls the patient twice during that window. The visit is then marked a no-show if the patient still doesn't join [1]. The 2025 policy used a 5-minute wait and one call [2].

## Does the rule vary by appointment type, clinic or provider?

I found no exceptions by appointment type, clinic or provider. The 2026 policy applies to in-person visits generally, and the 2025 policy said it applied "consistently at every clinic" [1][2]. The only exception in either version is the interpreter/accessibility one above.

I did not find a separate rule for specific clinicians or specialties. The policy also says the clinician may still see a late patient "if the schedule allows," so that is decided case by case.

## Do vendor scheduling systems enforce late-arrival handling?

I found no evidence that the scheduling system enforces late-arrival handling. The documents I found on the scheduling vendors cover other things:

- **ClearPath (scheduling):** The November 14, 2026 release includes a rule that blocks scheduling for patients in states where the clinician isn't licensed. This is a scheduling-time block, not a late-arrival rule [4][6][8].
- **Telehealth platform:** Its requirements cover join timing, such as visit links expiring 2 hours after the scheduled end time. They don't describe late-arrival rebooking [8].

So the 10-minute offer appears to be a front desk procedure rather than an automated system rule. I couldn't confirm whether ClearPath flags or auto-rebooks late patients. Someone who manages the scheduling system should confirm that.

## Gaps

- The knowledge base has no step-by-step script for the front desk on how to make the offer.
- I didn't find documentation on how late-arrival reschedules are recorded in the system.

**A large clinic needs 2.0 medical assistants for each physician or nurse practitioner on the schedule.** This is the current standard, effective September 1, 2026, and it replaces the 2025 version [1].

**Current standard (effective September 1, 2026)**

- A clinic is "large" when it averages more than 80 visits a day. The 2025 threshold was over 90 [1][2].
- A large clinic needs at least 3 physicians or NPs on site, 2.0 MAs per clinician, 2 RNs (one designated as charge nurse), and 4 front desk staff [1].
- The number of MAs is rounded up to the next whole person [1].
- At the 3-clinician minimum, that works out to at least 6 MAs on a large-clinic schedule (my calculation from the table).

**What changed from 2025**

The 2025 standard set large clinics at 1.5 MAs per clinician, with a threshold of over 90 visits a day [2]. The 2026 revision raised the ratio after a Q2 2026 operations review found that medium and large clinics were missing the door-to-room target on most afternoons [1].

**Other bands and sessions**

| Setting | MAs per clinician (2026 standard) |
|---|---|
| Small (under 40 visits/day) | 1.0 [1] |
| Medium (40–80 visits/day) | 1.5 [1] |
| Large (over 80 visits/day) | 2.0 [1] |
| Saturday session (any band) | 1.0 [1] |
| Sunday session (Harbor Point) | 1.0 [1] |

**Other factors**

- Band placement depends on visit volume, not specialty. Each clinic's band is set every quarter from the "Avg visits per day" column in the clinic directory, so a clinic can change bands when its volume changes [1][4].
- I found no separate ratio based on specialty.
- The Vendors collection has no MA-to-clinician ratios or staffing-software terms. Its documents cover vendor support, interpreting, billing and similar services [6][7][8].

**No.** Under the current staffing standard, a small clinic cannot run open hours without an RN on site. Every clinic, including small ones, must have at least one RN on site during open hours, and Saturday sessions also need one [2]. The 2025 standard that allowed small clinics to run without an RN was replaced on September 1, 2026 [2][1].

## The current rule for a small clinic

Small clinics are those averaging under 40 in-person visits a day [2]. The minimum on-site coverage for a small clinic is:

| Role | Minimum on site |
|---|---|
| Physician or NP | 1 |
| RN | 1 |
| Medical assistants | 1.0 per clinician |
| Front desk | 2 |

[2]

Your clinic's band comes from the "Avg visits per day" column in the clinic directory, which is recalculated every quarter. A clinic can move bands when its volume changes [4][2]. If your clinic's volume has grown past 40 a day, the medium-band minimums apply instead, which also require one RN [2].

## What to do when the RN is missing

The documents describe this process:

1. The clinic manager calls the float pool first. The float pool has two RNs on call each day [2].
2. If the float pool cannot cover, the clinic manager asks the regional medical director whether to reduce the schedule [2].
3. A session run without an RN must be reported in SafeReport as a near miss so QPS can track it [2].

A physician or NP must still be on site during open hours. If that coverage drops, the clinic manager contacts the float pool first, then converts in-person visits to telehealth where clinically appropriate [2][5].

The 2026 standard says clinics had until October 1, 2026 to reach the new minimums, and the float pool was increased by two RNs to cover the gap [2]. That window has now closed.

## Delegation when no RN is present

- **Medical assistants:** Under the 2026 standard, MAs give the Tier 1 items listed in the in-clinic formulary, under standing orders [2]. The formulary is narrower than it looks. Only some Tier 1 items list MA as an allowed giver: standard-dose and high-dose influenza, Tdap, and B12. COVID-19, PCV20, and medroxyprogesterone are RN or clinician only [6].
- **Physician or NP triage:** The 2025 standard had the physician or NP handle triage calls at small clinics without an RN [1]. The 2026 standard removes that arrangement and says small clinics without an RN were sending too many triage calls to the physician [2].
- **On-call RN access:** I found no clinic-level on-call RN procedure. The on-call rota covers medical directors, who are reached through the answering service, not an RN on-call service for clinics [7].
- **Telehealth triage RNs:** The telehealth front desk has two triage RNs [2]. The documents do not say these count toward on-site RN coverage.

## Vendor and staffing agency contracts

I found no staffing agency or nurse staffing contract in the Vendors collection. The vendor escalation matrix covers software and services such as Meridian, ClearPath, and Quillon, not nursing staff [8]. The float pool is an internal network resource, not a vendor [2].

## Sources that conflict

- The 2025 staffing standard allowed small clinics to run without an RN [1]. That is superseded.
- The PTO and clinic scheduling policy repeats only the physician or NP on-site rule, and does not mention RNs [5]. It does not override the staffing standard.

If your clinic is running or planning sessions without an RN, the staffing standard requires the float pool call and a SafeReport near-miss entry [2]. Clinical Operations is the owner of the standard and the place to confirm any exception [2][4].

The check goes live on **November 18, 2026**. The Clinical Systems Change Advisory Board (CSCAB) approved its release on October 28, 2026 [3].

**What the check is**

It is action 4 of the root cause analysis for RCA-26-07, the July incident in which 17 Bayline lab results were filed to the wrong patient's chart. The action is to add a positive patient identification check before results are released to the patient portal [1]. The project codename is **Heron**, owned by Clinical Informatics (Grace Oyelaran) [2].

**Dates in the sources**

| Source | Date or target | Status |
|---|---|---|
| RCA-26-07 action plan (Patient Safety Committee, reviewed Sept 10, 2026) | Due Nov 30, 2026 | In progress [1] |
| Digital projects register (updated Oct 19, 2026) | Target Q4 2026 | Build complete; awaiting release [2] |
| CSCAB minutes, CHG-2026-121 (Oct 28, 2026) | Release on Nov 18, 2026 | Approved [3] |

The CSCAB date is the most recent and is the actual release decision. The register says its "Target" column is only a planning quarter, and that CSCAB sets cutover and go-live dates [2]. The clinical safety sign-off was based on testing: in 400 test releases, every mismatched identifier was held for manual review [3].

**Rollout and conditions**

- I found no phased rollout, pilot, or deferred activation for this check in the Clinical Operations or Vendors documents I searched.
- CSCAB asked that Quality & Patient Safety (LP) receive a report of every result the check holds during the first two weeks after release. That report is due December 2, 2026 [3].
- The Patient Safety Committee asked for a status update on Heron at its December meeting [2].

**Don't confuse it with other dates**

- **February 6, 2027** is the cutover for the Wren project, the Meridian EHR upgrade. It is not the wrong-patient portal check [3].
- Wren's January 15, 2027 deadline is for retesting the Switchyard lab interfaces. That is separate from Heron [3].

The average Karen interpreter connection time last quarter (Q3 2026, July 1 to September 30) was **6 minutes 18 seconds** [1]. That is over Karen's 5-minute target by 1:18 [1][2].

**Q3 2026 Karen figures** [1]
- Average connect time: 6:18
- Sessions: 141
- Interpreted minutes: 2,690
- Dropped calls: 4.6%

Karen was the slowest of the languages listed in the report. Somali averaged 5:40, Haitian Creole 3:54, and all other languages combined 3:31 [1].

**How connect time is measured**
Connect time runs from the clinician pressing "Request interpreter" until the interpreter joins [1]. The report does not define a separate "Karen interpreter request."

**Targets and policy**
- Polyglen's service levels set a 5-minute target for Karen, because it is in the 5-minute tier. The top 20 languages and American Sign Language have a 2-minute target [1][2].
- Polyglen's P1 support response covers an interpreter not connecting at all. Slow connections within target are tracked in the quarterly language access report instead [3].
- Clinical Operations wants to add Haitian Creole and Karen to the 2-minute tier when the Polyglen contract renews. Renewal discussions start in November 2026, and the contract renews February 28, 2027 [2].

**Vendor**
Polyglen Interpreting provides the interpreting service, and the Clinical Operations report covers its visits [1][2].

**Caveats**
- The Q3 2026 report is the first quarterly report in this format. Earlier quarters were reported monthly by Polyglen and are not restated, so I could not compare Karen's trend [1].
- I found no interpreter connect-time policy in the People And Policy collection. The only connect-time statements there are general references to video interpreters connecting within 2 minutes [4][5].
- The report does not say whether the 6:18 average is weighted by session or by minute.

Sources: [1] Halcyon language access report, Q3 2026; [2] Polyglen Interpreting business associate record; [3] Halcyon vendor support and escalation matrix; [4] Patient intake procedure; [5] Approved AI tools for Halcyon staff.

A self-pay patient aged 65 or older pays **$72** for the 2026–27 high-dose flu shot at Halcyon clinics. That price includes the administration fee [1].

**Key details**
- **Eligibility:** The high-dose vaccine is for ages 65 and over. The 0.7 mL prefilled syringe can be given by an MA, RN or clinician [1].
- **Comparison:** The standard-dose flu shot (ages 6 months to 64) is $35 for self-pay patients [1].
- **Insured patients:** They are billed to their plan. The self-pay price applies only to uninsured and self-pay patients [1].

**Discounts**
- **Prompt-pay discount:** The 20% prompt-pay discount for self-pay patients does not apply to vaccine prices, which are already set at cost plus administration [1]. The general billing FAQ describes this 20% discount for self-pay visits [2], so the formulary is the more specific rule for vaccines.
- **Sliding-fee program:** Patients in the program receive the program discount on vaccines [1]. The sources do not give the exact percentage for vaccines. The program reduces visit costs by 40–100% [2], and the formulary does not say whether that range applies to vaccines.

**Vendor pricing**
I found no vendor contract or wholesaler price for the high-dose flu vaccine in the Vendors collection. The $72 figure comes from the clinic formulary, which is the only source I found that sets the self-pay price.

**The next monthly check on AED-NBR-01 is due November 10, 2026.** Its last check was October 10, 2026, and the unit is listed as in service [1]. That is 10 days from today.

**Where it is documented**
- AED-NBR-01 is a Vantor A3 at Northbridge (NBR) in the Q4 2026 emergency equipment inventory, compiled October 26, 2026 by Clinical Operations [1].

- The AED check confirms the self-test indicator is green, pads and battery are within date, and a spare pad set is present [1].

- Pads expire February 2027 and the battery in September 2027 [1]. Neither falls due before the November check.
- The Northbridge oxygen cylinder, OXY-NBR-01, is flagged "Action needed" at 450 psi, below the 500 psi minimum. A replacement has been requested [1]. This is a separate item from the AED.

**Conflicting timing in other documents**
I found no vendor or policy document that sets a different inspection interval for AED-NBR-01. The vendor support matrix covers contractual response times for live systems, not equipment inspections [8]. Vantor service repairs take 2–4 weeks, but that applies only after a unit fails [1]. The inventory is the only source I found that sets the check date, so it should be treated as the governing schedule. The inventory has no entry for a later check, so the November 10 date should stand unless the clinic manager records an earlier check.

rows.answer:
**ClearPath must respond to a P2 ticket within 4 hours.** Halcyon's vendor support and escalation matrix sets this target [1]. I did not find a separate ClearPath contract in the knowledge base, so this is Halcyon's internal target rather than confirmed contract language.

**How P2 is defined**
- P2 means a major function is degraded but a workaround exists [1].
- P1 is a system that is down or unusable at one or more clinics, or any problem that creates a patient-safety risk. P3 covers minor, single-user issues and questions [1].

**Timing details to watch**
- ClearPath's support hours are 24/7 for P1 only. Everything else, including P2, is covered 07:00–19:00 Eastern, Monday to Friday [1].
- The matrix does not say how the 4-hour window counts when a ticket arrives outside those hours. Today is Saturday, so a P2 raised now would fall outside support hours until Monday, November 2 at 07:00 Eastern. Confirm the counting rule with the Service Desk.
- For comparison, the matrix gives ClearPath a 30-minute P1 response and a 2-business-day P3 response [1].

**Escalation**
- Staff should open a ticket with the IT Service Desk (extension 4357 or the intranet tile). The Service Desk contacts the vendor and tracks the response against the matrix. Clinic staff should not call vendors directly unless the Service Desk asks them to [1].
- The matrix describes escalation for missed responses only for P1. The Service Desk escalates to the vendor's account manager and tells the owning team's steward. Two missed P1 responses in a quarter are reported to the HIPAA Security Officer and recorded in the vendor's annual review [1]. I found no equivalent rule for P2 misses.
- The matrix lists no P2-specific exceptions or amendments for ClearPath. The only ClearPath-specific note I found is that its RCM team owns the system [1].

rows.answer:
The knowledge base does not contain a self-pay price for the RSV vaccine, so I can't give a number.

**What I found**

- Halcyon's in-clinic vaccine formulary (2026–27) lists self-pay prices for 14 vaccines and injectables, but RSV is not one of them [1]. Its scope note says anything not on the list cannot be given in clinic without approval from the Pharmacy and Therapeutics subcommittee [1]. RSV may therefore not be an in-clinic vaccine at all, or it may need a special approval.
- No chargemaster entry, vendor contract, or pricing exception for RSV appeared in my searches of the clinical, people-and-policy, and vendor collections.

**Related pricing rules that would apply to a self-pay vaccine**

- For listed vaccines, the self-pay price includes the administration fee [1]. Unlisted vaccines would need a price from the pharmacy team.
- The 20% prompt-pay discount does not apply to vaccine and injectable prices [1]. The prompt-pay discount applies to visit fees [2].
- Patients in the sliding-fee program receive the program discount on vaccines [1]. Patients with household income under 250% of the federal poverty level qualify, and front desk staff can start the application at check-in [2].
- Uninsured and self-pay patients receive a good-faith estimate at least one business day before a scheduled service, or three business days if it is scheduled 10 or more days out [2]. This is the mechanism for quoting the RSV price before the visit.
- If a vaccine is not stocked, Tier 3 items are ordered for a named patient from the wholesaler and take about 5 business days [1].

**Suggested next step:** Ask the clinical pharmacist, Dr. Farah Qureshi, or the Pharmacy and Therapeutics subcommittee whether RSV vaccine is approved for in-clinic use and what the self-pay price is [1]. The billing team can then issue the good-faith estimate [2].

**I can't find an average connect time for Karen interpreters in Q2 2026.** The knowledge base only has a Karen figure for Q3 2026 (July–September): 6 minutes 18 seconds. That is the closest available number, but it is not the Q2 figure you asked for.

**What the Q3 2026 report shows for Karen**

- Average connect time: 6:18, based on 141 sessions and 2,690 interpreted minutes [1].
- Dropped calls: 4.6% [1].
- Karen is in the 5-minute tier, which targets connection within 5 minutes [1]. The 6:18 average is above that target [1].

**Why Q2 is missing**

- The Q3 report is described as the first quarterly report in this format. Earlier quarters were reported monthly by Polyglen and are not restated in it [1].
- I searched for Polyglen monthly reports and Q2 language access reports and found none in the knowledge base.

**Other collections checked**

- **Vendors:** The Polyglen business associate record sets the connect-time targets (2 minutes for the top 20 languages, 5 minutes for others) and says Polyglen sends a monthly quality report with connect times to Clinical Operations [2]. It does not give Karen figures. It also notes that Clinical Operations wants to add Karen to the 2-minute tier at the November 2026 renewal discussion [2].
- **Vendors (escalation matrix):** It says slow connections within target are tracked in the quarterly language access report, not in vendor support escalations [3].
- **People And Policy:** I found no methodology for calculating average connect time. The only definition I found is in the Clinical Operations Q3 report: connect time runs from when the clinician presses "Request interpreter" until the interpreter joins, and averages are shown as minutes:seconds [1].

**Next step**

The monthly Polyglen quality reports for April–June 2026 would contain the Q2 Karen figures. The Polyglen account is owned by Rosa Delgado in Clinical Operations [2], so she is the most likely source for those reports.

**Short answer:** The knowledge base sets no response time for Tallgrass Survey. Tallgrass isn't a live Halcyon vendor, so it has no support SLA on record.

**Why there's no SLA**

- Tallgrass Survey Co. is a proposed business associate (record BA-021). Its business associate agreement is not executed. The draft arrived in August 2026, and the signed order form is on hold until the BAA is signed [1].
- The Halcyon vendor support and escalation matrix covers only outside vendors that support live Halcyon systems. It states that vendors not yet supporting a live system are not listed, and that their support terms are agreed when the contract is signed [3]. Tallgrass does not appear in the matrix.

**What would apply once Tallgrass is live**

I found no Tallgrass-specific support terms, amendments, escalation clauses or priority tiers. The only applicable framework is the general matrix, which currently has these priorities:

- **P1** (system down or unusable at one or more clinics, or a patient-safety risk): a vendor's first response is due within the time in its row. For example, Meridian is 15 minutes, Polyglen 10 minutes, and RotaLeaf 4 hours [3].
- **P2** (major function degraded, workaround exists) and **P3** (minor issues, single-user questions) have their own response windows in the matrix [3].
- Response times are first responses from a qualified engineer, not resolution times [3].
- Staff should open a ticket with the IT Service Desk (ext. 4357) rather than calling the vendor directly. The Service Desk tracks vendor response times against the matrix [3].

Whatever terms are agreed for Tallgrass would need to be added to the matrix, since the matrix is the document that tracks them.

**Related timing**

- No PHI may be shared with Tallgrass until the BAA is signed, including for test files or pilots [1].
- The privacy officer is due to send revised retention language by November 6, 2026. The 5-year vs. 18-month retention dispute is still open [1].
- If the BAA isn't signed by January 31, 2027, the Quality & Patient Safety team will look at other survey vendors [1].
- Until then, post-visit surveys for Juniper and in-person visits use the in-app survey in the Halcyon app. The steering committee plans to switch to Tallgrass once its BAA is signed [1][2].

The knowledge base doesn't state how much a physician is paid for a week on the on-call medical director rota. I found no pay rate, stipend, or per-shift or weekly rate for this role.

**What the rota does say**
- Coverage runs in weekly blocks, Monday 08:00 to the following Monday 08:00 Eastern. The November 2026 rota lists Dr. Priya Natarajan, Dr. Helen Mwangi, Dr. Samuel Achterberg, Dr. Luis Carvalho and Dr. Ingrid Solberg as on-call medical directors, with backups [1].
- The role is the senior physician on duty for the whole network. Duties include receiving critical lab results when the ordering clinician can't be reached, being notified of sentinel events, approving emergency clinical system changes, and advising on transfers and closures [1][2][5].
- Swaps must be agreed by both physicians and logged with the Office of the CMO at least 72 hours ahead [1].

**Related pay information that doesn't cover this role**
- Staff who work on a holiday receive 1.5× pay plus a floating holiday [4]. The source doesn't say whether this applies to on-call medical director shifts.
- Clinical staff receive $2,000 per year for continuing medical education, plus 5 days of paid CME time [6]. This is not on-call pay.

**Vendor contracts**
The vendor support matrix covers system support response times only. It doesn't cover physician on-call coverage or payment [3].

To get the figure, ask the Office of the Chief Medical Officer, which owns the rota [1], or the People team for the compensation terms.

I couldn't find a bereavement leave policy for Halcyon Health, so I can't give a number of days. I searched the People And Policy, Clinical Operations and Vendors collections with several phrasings (bereavement, compassionate leave, funeral leave, death in the family, grief leave) and found nothing on it.

The closest entitlements in the knowledge base are:

- **Annual leave:** Full-time staff accrue 20 days per year in years 1–3 and 25 days from year 4. This replaced the old PTO rules on October 1, 2026 [9][8]. Annual leave is not specific to bereavement.
- **Sick leave:** Sick time is separate from PTO at 48 hours per year, available from day one [8]. The documents don't say whether bereavement absences can be charged to it.

Nothing in the Clinical Operations or Vendors documents I found changes leave entitlements. The vendor matrix lists RotaLeaf as the HR and leave system [3], and the digital projects register notes that leave requests now go through RotaLeaf [4]. Neither mentions bereavement.

To get the answer, ask the People team, since they own the annual leave policy [9]. They can confirm whether a separate bereavement policy exists and what applies to immediate and extended family.

Yes. Halcyon pairs every new clinical hire with a preceptor for 90 days, which is the closest equivalent to Northwind's onboarding buddy [6]. I couldn't find a stated duration for the Northwind buddy, so the two programs can't be compared on length.

**Halcyon Health: preceptor program for new clinicians**
- **Duration:** 90 days [6].
- **Check-ins:** Weekly for the first month, then every other week [6].
- **Competency sign-offs:** The preceptor signs off on the clinician's competency checklist at 30, 60 and 90 days [6].
- **Early days:** On days 4–5, new clinicians shadow at their home clinic with the preceptor [6].

**Northwind Labs: onboarding buddy**
- The welcome guide says the new hire's manager and onboarding buddy will walk them through the first two weeks [1].
- The buddy suggests names for the 1:1s new hires should schedule with at least five people outside their team [1].
- The sources I found don't say how long the buddy relationship lasts [1].

**How they differ**
- Halcyon's preceptor support is a defined 90-day program with set check-in cadence and formal competency milestones [6]. Northwind's buddy role is described only for the first two weeks, and no milestones are mentioned [1].
- Halcyon's program is written for clinical hires. Its onboarding also includes credentialing, which takes 30 to 60 days, and clinicians can't see patients until their licenses, DEA registration (where applicable) and board certification are verified [6].

If you need Northwind's buddy duration confirmed, check with Northwind's People team, since it isn't in the onboarding materials I searched.

**Short answer:** I found no Northwind equivalent to Halcyon's PHI systems inventory. Northwind's knowledge base doesn't mention PHI or HIPAA, and no document lists which Northwind systems hold regulated data alongside an owning team. Northwind does keep several partial registers, and each has a different owner.

## Northwind's closest equivalents

- **Production cell inventory:** Lists every data-plane cell, its region, data residency and status. It is maintained by the Platform team (PLAT) and was last updated October 23, 2026 [7]. It covers where customer event data lives, not which systems hold sensitive data.
- **Vendor register:** Each vendor record has a data class, a "Customer data?" field, a DPA status and a business owner. For example, Parcelwise (transactional email) is marked as receiving customer names and email addresses, with the Parcelwise register entry noting that questions about what is sent should go to the team that owns the source system [14]. Saltmarsh (product analytics) is owned by Product, with Mateo Alvarez as business owner [8].
- **Data classification:** The information security policy, owned by the Security team, defines four classes (Restricted, Confidential, Internal, Public) and their handling rules. Restricted covers customer event payloads, credentials and encryption keys [6].
- **Customer data retention standard:** Owned by the Security team. It maps each data type to where it lives (for example, Kafka hot buffer, cold store, Lookout logs, Atlas workspace metadata) and sets default retention periods [11].

## Who maintains what

- **Security team:** Owns the information security policy and the retention standard [6][11].
- **Platform team:** Maintains the cell inventory [7].
- **Product:** Owns the Saltmarsh vendor record [8].
- **Service catalog:** Northwind's documents say the service catalog lists which team owns each service [7][13]. I could not find the catalog in the knowledge base, so I can't confirm its contents or maintainer.

## Halcyon for comparison

Halcyon's inventory is maintained by the HIPAA Security Officer, Ahmed Siddiqui. It is reviewed quarterly, with the last review on October 1, 2026, and it lists owning teams by code [1]. The HIPAA policy treats it as the approved list of systems for PHI [1][5]. The project register adds a control: when a project closes, the lead updates the systems inventory if a new system now holds PHI [3].

Northwind's vendor register is the closest thing to Halcyon's process. It records what data each vendor touches and whether customer data is involved. It is not a PHI-specific list, and I found no evidence that Northwind's vendor or support documents reference a process like Halcyon's.

If you want Northwind to have a PHI-equivalent list, the Security team would be the right owner to ask, since it already owns the data classification and retention documents. I'd also check with them whether the service catalog covers this, as I could not locate it.

**Short answer:** Patient incidents at Halcyon go into **SafeReport**. Anyone involved in or who witnessed the event files the report, and the policy sets the deadline at **within 24 hours**. Tell the charge nurse on shift right away, because the immediate response comes before the report. Northwind's `/incident declare` is for production and service incidents and doesn't apply to patient events.

## Where it gets logged

- Patient safety events are reported in **SafeReport** [8].
- Software-caused events, such as the duplicate medication reminders, also follow this policy. Fixes then go through clinical systems change control [8][10].
- Privacy incidents are a separate track. Report them to the Privacy Officer within 24 hours at privacy@halcyon.example or through the compliance hotline [9].

## Who files and how fast

**Immediately** [8]:
1. Make the patient safe and follow the clinical escalation protocol. Call 911 if needed.
2. Tell the charge nurse on shift. In clinics without one, tell the clinic manager.
3. For a sentinel event, the charge nurse notifies the on-call medical director within 1 hour.

The charge nurse then coordinates the response, including who stays with the patient, who calls the family, and who secures equipment, medications or records [8].

**Within 24 hours** [8]:
- Anyone involved or who witnessed the event files a SafeReport. Reporting is never optional and never punished.
- The attending clinician discloses the event to the patient or family, with the charge nurse or medical director present.

The policy doesn't name one specific filer. The obligation falls on everyone involved or who witnessed the event. The 24-hour deadline comes from the policy section heading, so confirm it with Quality & Patient Safety if you need the exact wording.

**If you're unsure of the level,** report at the higher one. Quality & Patient Safety will reclassify if needed [8].

**Follow-up:**
- Every Level 1 (sentinel) and Level 2 event gets a root cause analysis. QPS charters the team within 72 hours, and the RCA must be completed within 45 calendar days of the event becoming known [8].
- Completed RCAs go to the Patient Safety Committee, chaired by Dr. Kenji Watanabe [8].

**Other reporting examples:**
- A vaccine refrigerator outside 2–8 °C: call the clinical pharmacist within 1 hour, then file a SafeReport [13].
- A clinic session run without an RN: file a SafeReport as a near miss [14].

## Comparison with Northwind's `/incident declare`

| | Halcyon (patient event) | Northwind (production incident) |
|---|---|---|
| Entry point | SafeReport, plus telling the charge nurse | `/incident declare` in Slack [1] |
| Who is alerted | Charge nurse, then on-call medical director for sentinel events [8] | Incident commander rotation is paged; the channel and timeline are opened [1][2][6] |
| Severity | Levels 1–4, from sentinel event to near miss [8] | SEV-1 to SEV-3 [1] |
| Urgent deadline | Medical director within 1 hour for sentinel events [8] | SEV-1: IC assigned within 15 minutes; first status page update within 20 minutes [1][2] |
| Filing deadline | Within 24 hours [8] | Postmortem for SEV-1/SEV-2 within 5 business days of resolution [2] |
| Root cause review | RCA within 45 days for Level 1–2 events [8] | Blameless postmortem; reviewed at the Thursday reliability meeting [2] |

The two processes are parallel. Northwind's workflow runs through a Slack command and an on-call rotation. Halcyon's runs through a charge nurse and a reporting system. The sources don't describe a Halcyon equivalent of the slash command.

**Technical side at Halcyon:** If the problem is a system or vendor issue, open a ticket with the IT Service Desk (ext. 4357). A problem that creates a patient-safety risk, such as results not arriving, is a P1 [12]. The Service Desk handles vendor contact, so clinic staff shouldn't call vendors directly unless asked [12].

**Short answer:** Northwind reviews incidents in the same spirit as Halcyon's just-culture RCAs, but it calls its approach "blameless," not "just culture." The author is chosen by the incident commander for each incident, usually the responder who knew the most about the failure. Halcyon's RCAs are chartered by Quality & Patient Safety and led by a named QPS lead.

**Northwind Labs**

- **Standard:** Every SEV-1 and SEV-2 incident needs a blameless postmortem within five business days of resolution [1][2][3]. The FAQ says postmortems look at "the system and the process, not at individuals," and names appear only in the timeline [2].
- **Review forum:** Postmortems are reviewed at the Thursday reliability meeting [2][3].
- **Who writes it:** The incident commander (IC) picks the author, "usually the responder who knew the most about the failure" [2]. Responders are the engineers from the owning team who investigate and fix [2].
- **Example:** The INC-2291 ingest outage postmortem was written by Priya Raman with the ingest team [5]. The IC for that incident was Oluwaseun Adeyemi [1].

**Halcyon Health**

- **Standard:** Every Level 1 and Level 2 event gets an RCA. The policy says RCAs "use a just-culture approach: we look for system causes, not someone to blame" [8].
- **Who writes it:** QPS charters the RCA team within 72 hours, and the RCA must be completed within 45 calendar days [8]. For RCA-26-07, the RCA lead was Lorraine Pike of Quality & Patient Safety [9]. The sources don't describe the team's full makeup.
- **Review forum:** Completed RCAs and their action plans go to the Patient Safety Committee, chaired by CMO Dr. Kenji Watanabe. The committee tracks every action item to closure [8].
- **Example:** RCA-26-07 was completed August 28, 2026, 36 days after the event became known on July 23 [9]. Its root causes were system-focused: fallback matching rule, no monitoring of fallback matches, and no change-notice obligation in the lab agreement [9].

**Comparison**

| | Northwind Labs | Halcyon Health |
|---|---|---|
| Framing | Blameless postmortem [2][3] | Just-culture RCA [8] |
| Scope | SEV-1 and SEV-2 [1][2] | Level 1 and Level 2 events [8] |
| Deadline | 5 business days after resolution [2] | 45 calendar days after the event became known [8] |
| Author | Chosen per incident by the IC, usually the most knowledgeable responder [2] | RCA team chartered by QPS, with a QPS lead [8][9] |
| Oversight | Thursday reliability meeting [2][3] | Patient Safety Committee, monthly [8] |

**Gaps**

- I found no Northwind document that defines a postmortem template, a formal author role, or an explicit just-culture policy. The Engineering and Support material I searched covered incident roles and deadlines, not a template [1][2][3].
- I found no Halcyon document that spells out RCA team membership beyond the QPS charter and lead [8][9].

**Short answer:** Northwind has a quarterly access review with automatic revocation, but that policy covers Northwind's own production and customer-data systems, not EHR access. The EHR access controls I found belong to Halcyon Health, and they cover monthly log review rather than periodic recertification of who still needs access. The knowledge base does not say what happens at Halcyon if an access review is never signed off.

## Northwind Labs

- **Review cadence and owner:** Quarterly access reviews are run by each team lead [8].
- **If access is not re-confirmed:** It is revoked automatically [8].
- **Other access limits:**
  - Production access is granted through Teleport and expires after 8 hours. Standing access to production databases is not allowed for anyone [8].
  - Leavers lose all access within one hour of their final working time [8].
  - Policy exceptions need written approval from the Head of Security and expire after 90 days [8].
  - Emergency access to customer workspaces expires after 2 hours and needs a second engineer's approval in Teleport [9].
- **Gaps:** The policy does not say how a review is documented, whether managers or anyone other than the team lead must sign off, or whether there is an escalation step before revocation. It was last reviewed in July 2026 [8].

## Halcyon Health (EHR)

- **Log review:** The compliance team reviews EHR access logs monthly using automated anomaly detection. Unusual access triggers a review with the employee's manager [3].
- **Training-based suspension:** Clinical system access is suspended automatically if HIPAA training is more than 14 days overdue [3].
- **Break-the-glass:** Staff can open a chart outside their normal patient relationships in an emergency. No one approves it in the moment, and access lasts until the end of the shift, up to 12 hours [7].
- **Recertification:** I found no documented periodic review of whether EHR users still need their access, and no documented revocation or escalation if such a review is missed.

## Does anything conflict?

No direct conflict, because the two policies govern different systems. Northwind's policy does not cover Halcyon's EHR [8]. Halcyon's vendor escalation matrix covers vendor support response times, not access reviews [6].

## Suggested next steps

- Confirm with the Privacy Officer (Margaret Holloway) or the HIPAA Security Officer (Ahmed Siddiqui) whether Halcyon has an unpublished periodic access recertification process. The knowledge base does not show one [3][4].
- If your question is about Northwind's own systems, ask the Northwind Security team how the team-lead quarterly review is evidenced and what happens at the sign-off stage.

**Short answer:** Halcyon requires four things before staff can use a new AI tool with patient data. The usual wait is 6–10 weeks, mostly spent waiting on the BAA. Northwind's knowledge base says that a tool processing customer data must clear `#vendor-review` first, but it doesn't say how long that review takes. The two processes are separate, and the documents don't show one depending on the other.

**Northwind's `#vendor-review` process**

- Any tool that will process customer data, or that costs more than $50 per month, must go through the `#vendor-review` security review before it's used [1].
- The knowledge base doesn't give a typical duration or service level for this review.
- Vendor register entries show what a review can produce. Hollowpine Helpdesk got a conditional pass: its AI reply suggestions must stay disabled until its Data Processing Agreement (DPA) is signed. It is also running under a security exception, SEC-EX-117 [2].
- Other entries record passed reviews, DPAs and SOC 2 reports, and a "re-reviewed" status for some vendors [3][4][5].

**What Halcyon requires for AI tools that handle PHI**

Any tool that will handle protected health information needs [8]:

1. A security risk assessment.
2. A signed business associate agreement (BAA) with the vendor.
3. An entry in the clinical and business systems inventory [8][11].
4. For clinical use, a clinical safety review by the CMIO [8].

Requests go by email to the Privacy Officer (Margaret Holloway) and the HIPAA Security Officer (Ahmed Siddiqui) [8]. Two further rules apply:

- No PHI may be shared with a vendor until its BAA is executed. This includes test files or "just a few names" for a pilot [14].
- Only tools on the approved list may take PHI. Other AI scribes are not approved, even for trials [8][9].

**How long it takes at Halcyon**

- The published typical turnaround is 6–10 weeks, mostly waiting on the BAA [8].
- Quillon Ambient, the approved AI scribe, is an example. Its BAA was executed July 30, 2026, its risk assessment was completed in July, and the pilot started August 17 at two clinics [9].
- Expanding a tool beyond its pilot clinics requires a CSCAB decision and a clinical safety review [9].
- The CSCAB reminded the board on October 28, 2026 that any project adding a new place to store PHI needs its risk assessment and inventory entry before go-live, not after [13].

**How the two relate**

- Halcyon's requirements apply to Halcyon staff and PHI. Northwind's `#vendor-review` applies to Northwind's own customer data. Nothing in either knowledge base makes one depend on the other.
- If your tool will touch Halcyon patient data, Halcyon's four requirements apply regardless of Northwind's review outcome.
- Northwind's leadership notes say the company declined an acquisition of a healthcare analytics startup because of "HIPAA obligations we are not set up for" [18]. Nothing in Northwind's documents describes a BAA or HIPAA process, so you should check with Halcyon's Privacy Officer before sending PHI to any Northwind-run tool.

**Short answer:** Halcyon's equivalent is the system steward for Digital Health Engineering, Patient Engagement (DHE-PE), currently Felix Brandt. For a purely cosmetic change, his approval is enough under the written policy. Confirm first that the change really is cosmetic.

**Who owns it**
- The Halcyon app, which includes bill pay, is owned by DHE-PE [13]. The app holds intake forms and insurance card images [13].
- Each owning team has one system steward who approves changes to that team's systems. For DHE-PE, that is Felix Brandt [7].

**Is his approval enough?**
- The policy defines minor changes as "cosmetic changes, report tweaks, adding a user," and says these need "steward approval only" [7].
- Significant changes need three approvals: the steward, a clinical safety sign-off from the CMIO (Dr. Anjali Rao, or delegate Dr. Benedict Osei), and review at the weekly Clinical Systems Change Advisory Board (CSCAB) [7].
- Significant changes are those affecting patient-facing automation, the patient app's clinical content, medication information, orders or results routing, clinical decision support, or scheduler/job-runner cutovers [7]. A cosmetic tweak to bill pay should not fall into these categories, so it would be minor.
- I found no separate privacy, HIPAA or compliance sign-off requirement for minor UI changes in the documents I searched.

**Things to check before you rely on that**
- Whether the change is truly cosmetic. The policy gives examples but no formal definition, so the classification is a judgment call. If the tweak touches anything clinical, medication, or patient-facing automation, it becomes significant [7].
- Changes made without the required approvals are reported to QPS as safety events [7]. Getting the steward's written sign-off protects you here.
- The policy names no delegate for the DHE-PE steward role, unlike the CMIO role. Confirm with Felix Brandt who covers when he is out.

**How this compares with Northwind**
- At Northwind, normal production changes need the owning team's change approver, and approvals are valid for 7 days [1][6]. Felix Brandt's role maps to that approver.
- Northwind's policy lists examples of normal changes (schema migrations, infrastructure config, retention settings, and auth or billing logic), and a cosmetic UI change is not among them. Its standard changes are pre-approved and need only normal PR review [1]. So a cosmetic UI tweak at Northwind may need only a reviewed PR, unless it touches billing logic. In that case, the handbook requires two approvals, one from a code owner [2]. Confirm with your Northwind team before assuming either way.

rows.answer:
**Short answer:** Both fixes make the job safe to re-run. Northwind made invoice creation idempotent per workspace and billing period. Halcyon gave each reminder an idempotency key and added rules for scheduler cutovers. Neither organization's documents describe a fix that stops two systems from running the same job at the same time. Halcyon's rule only requires a written runbook for that.

## Northwind Labs: duplicate September invoices (INC-2340, October 6)

**Root cause:** The payment provider's webhook for the first batch timed out at 06:05. The retry logic re-ran the batch, and invoice creation wasn't idempotent [8]. The job ran twice for some workspaces, producing 312 duplicate invoices across 287 workspaces. 201 of those were auto-charged [8].

**Technical fix:**
- An idempotency key per (workspace, billing period) on invoice creation. It was merged and deployed the same day, and a dry run showed zero duplicates [8].
- The changelog lists it as shipped October 8 [9]. The October 26 status report also marks it done [11].

**Other follow-ups:**
- A daily reconciliation report comparing invoices with charges is marked done [11].
- An alert for provider webhook timeouts during a billing batch is still open, due November 6 [11].
- The invoice history view now hides voided duplicates [11].
- Before the new payment provider cuts over on January 19, 2027, its webhook handler must be made idempotent, because the new provider retries faster [11].

**Documentation gap:** The incident log says a full postmortem was published October 13 [10]. I could not find that postmortem in the knowledge base. The fix details above come from the Slack incident export, the changelog, and the status report. The postmortem itself should be checked for its formal action items and owners.

## Halcyon Health: duplicate medication reminders (IR-0412, September 3)

**Root cause:** A September 2 configuration change moved the reminder scheduler to a new job runner. During cutover, the old and new runners were both active. Neither checked whether a reminder had already been sent, because the old system assumed it was the only sender [1]. Reminders went out two to four times to 2,318 patients, and 12 patients reported taking an extra dose. None needed treatment [1].

**Technical fix:**
- Reminders now carry an idempotency key of (patient, medication, scheduled time). A reminder with an existing key is never sent again [1].
- The Marigold acknowledgement message follows the same rule, with an idempotency key on every message [14].

**Process fixes:**
- Scheduler or job-runner cutovers require a written runbook that states how double-running is prevented, plus clinical safety sign-off [1][2].
- The Clinical Systems Change Advisory Board's change control policy now lists scheduler cutovers as significant changes, which require steward approval, CMIO clinical safety sign-off, and CSCAB review [2].
- Reminder text now says "If you already took this dose, you don't need to take it again" [1].

**Gap:** The Halcyon review does not list owners, due dates, or a monitoring alert for duplicate sends. The fix is documented as done, but the review doesn't show how it was verified.

## Comparison

| | Northwind (INC-2340) | Halcyon (IR-0412) |
|---|---|---|
| Duplicate mechanism | Retry re-ran a batch | Two active runners during cutover |
| Idempotency control | Per workspace and billing period, on invoice creation [8][9] | Per patient, medication and scheduled time, on each reminder [1] |
| Control on cutovers or retries | Idempotent handler required before the January 2027 provider cutover [11] | Runbook and clinical sign-off required for cutovers [1][2] |
| Open items | Webhook-timeout alert due Nov 6 [11] | None listed; no owners or verification recorded [1] |

**Short answer:** At Northwind Labs, health coverage starts on your first day. At Halcyon Health, it starts on the first of the month after your start date, so it can be up to about a month later.

**Northwind Labs:** Health, dental and vision coverage "starts on your first day" [1]. The onboarding guide doesn't mention a waiting period or enrollment deadline.

**Halcyon Health:** "Medical, dental and vision coverage begins on the first of the month after your start date" [2]. For example, a start date of November 2 would mean coverage begins December 1. The guide doesn't say how a start on the 1st is treated, so confirm that with HR. Clinical hires also face credentialing, which takes 30 to 60 days and sets the start date [2]. That means a clinical hire's wait for coverage is usually longer than the first-of-month rule alone suggests, because the start date itself is pushed back.

**Waiting periods, enrollment deadlines and conditions:** I found no waiting period, enrollment window or eligibility condition for either company. The Northwind guide also says nothing about a probation period, and it is an onboarding guide rather than a plan document, so the full plan terms may differ.

**Carrier and plan effective dates:** The knowledge base has no insurance carrier contract or plan effective date for either company's employee plans. The Halcyon vendor records I found cover billing, survey and support vendors, not benefits carriers [11][12][14]. The Northwind vendor collection didn't surface anything relevant either.

**Other benefit notes:**
- Halcyon offers a $1,800 annual HSA contribution if you choose the high-deductible plan [2].
- Northwind's first-day coverage is paired with a 401(k) with a 4% match that vests immediately [1].

To confirm the exact dates and any enrollment rules, ask each company's People team for the plan documents.

rows.answer:
**Short answer:** Northwind Labs has a formal holiday change freeze from December 18, 2026 to January 4, 2027. Halcyon Health has no IT change freeze over the holidays, based on the documents I found.

## Northwind Labs

**Holiday freeze: December 18, 2026 to January 4, 2027.** Only standard and emergency changes ship during this period [1]. Standard changes are pre-approved and need only a normal PR review. Examples include scaling, flipping an already-rolled-out feature flag, and restarting a runner pod [1].

Other Northwind rules that matter for holiday planning:

- **Rollbacks are allowed at any time, freeze or not** [1][3].
- **Month-end billing freeze:** no normal changes to Ledger from the last business day of the month until invoices are sent, usually the 2nd [1][4]. The current window runs from Friday, October 30, until invoices go out, expected November 2 [4].
- **Deploy window:** Monday through Thursday, 09:00–16:00 Pacific. Friday deploys need approval from the on-call engineering manager [3].
- **Exceptions:** if the change approver and delegate are both unavailable, the VP Engineering may approve. Exceptions are logged in `#eng-changes` [1].
- **Staffing:** the on-call rota marks the week of December 22 as inside the holiday change freeze. The rota for shifts starting December 29 onward will be published by December 15 [2].
- **Thanksgiving week:** Harriet Vance and Arjun Mehta, who are the Identity & Billing approvers, are both out November 24–27. Plan normal changes to Ledger or Keystone around that, or use the exceptions route [4][5].

## Halcyon Health

I found no formal holiday change-freeze policy for Halcyon. The most direct statement is in the October 2026 Juniper steering committee notes: "No IT freeze at Halcyon, but clinic managers asked that pilot training not land in the week of December 21" [6]. That note is from a project steering committee, not a company-wide change policy, so you may want to confirm it with the CMIO's office or the Clinical Systems Change Advisory Board (CSCAB).

Halcyon-specific holiday dates to plan around:

- **Week of December 21:** clinic managers asked that Juniper pilot training avoid this week [6].
- **Juniper go/no-go:** December 16 steering meeting [6].
- **Juniper pilot:** January 12, 2027 at Riverside, Elm Park and Northgate [6].
- **Annual leave:** staffing for Thanksgiving week and December 20 to January 2 is allocated on a rotating basis, which affects who is available [7].

Any significant change still needs three approvals: the system steward, clinical safety sign-off from the CMIO (or Associate CMIO Dr. Benedict Osei), and CSCAB review. CSCAB meets Wednesdays at 14:00 Eastern [8]. Clinical systems changes that touch patient-facing automation, medication information, results routing, or scheduler cutovers fall under this process [8]. The next major cutover, a scheduled Saturday, February 6, 2027 change, has its final go/no-go at CSCAB on January 27, 2027 [12].

## Comparison

| | Northwind Labs | Halcyon Health |
|---|---|---|
| Holiday freeze | Dec 18, 2026 – Jan 4, 2027 [1] | None found; "No IT freeze" noted [6] |
| Allowed during freeze | Standard and emergency changes [1] | Not applicable |
| Other dates to avoid | Ledger month-end billing freeze [1][4] | Week of Dec 21 for pilot training [6] |

rows.answer:
**Short answer:** At both organizations, when you're unsure, rate higher. Northwind's incident commander can change a severity at any time. At Halcyon, QPS reclassifies events, but the policy doesn't name a person or a downgrade process.

## Northwind Labs (incidents)

- **Rating when impact is unclear:** Declare higher. The incident FAQ says, "When unsure, declare higher; downgrading is cheap" [4].
- **Who sets it first:** "Whoever declares picks an initial severity" [4].
- **Who can change it later:** "The IC can raise or lower it at any time" [4]. The incident commander rotation is Kofi Mensah, Priya Raman, Harriet Vance, Oluwaseun Adeyemi and Ravi Subramanian [12].
- **Related rules:** SEV-1 covers data loss or a full ingest or pipeline outage for a cell. SEV-2 covers partial outages or degradation affecting many customers [1]. Every SEV-1 and SEV-2 needs a blameless postmortem within five business days [4].

The on-call runbook defines the levels but has no unclear-impact guidance [1]. The "declare higher" rule and IC authority come from the Incident roles FAQ, an informal onboarding document [4]. The sources don't say whether anyone other than the IC can change a severity during an incident.

## Halcyon Health (patient safety events)

- **Rating when severity is uncertain:** The Sentinel and adverse event reporting policy says, "When unsure, report at the higher level. QPS will reclassify if needed" [2]. Here "higher" means the more serious level: Level 1 is a sentinel event, and Level 4 is a near miss [2].
- **Who can change it later:** Quality & Patient Safety (QPS) reclassifies events [2]. The RCA lead for RCA-26-07 was Lorraine Pike of QPS [7], but the sources don't say she has reclassification authority.
- **Oversight:** The Patient Safety Committee, chaired by CMO Dr. Kenji Watanabe, reviews completed RCAs and tracks action items [2]. The sources don't say the committee approves rating changes.
- **Decisions about external reporting:** QPS decides whether an event is reported to a state health department or accrediting body [2].

The policy doesn't say who in QPS can downgrade an event, what justification is needed, or whether changes must be documented. Check with QPS directly before relying on a downgrade.

## Gaps

- Northwind: no written rule on who besides the IC can change a severity.
- Halcyon: no named role or documented process for reclassifying or downgrading an event.

**Short answer:** Northwind's helpdesk vendor (Hollowpine) is stuck on how it can use customer ticket content, specifically AI training. Halcyon's patient survey vendor (Tallgrass) is stuck on how long identifiable survey responses can be kept.

## Northwind Labs: Hollowpine Helpdesk

Hollowpine Software Co. provides Northwind's customer support ticketing and help center. Its DPA is not signed. The draft arrived in July 2026, and redlines have been with legal since August [1].

The main open point is Hollowpine's right to use ticket content to train its reply-suggestion model [1]. Until the DPA is signed:

- Hollowpine is running under security exception SEC-EX-117, approved by the Head of Security on August 24, 2026 [1].
- The security review is a conditional pass. AI reply suggestions must stay disabled until the DPA is signed [1].
- If the DPA is still unsigned when the exception lapses, Support Operations must either renew the exception or move ticket intake back to email [1].

Northwind's policy says exceptions expire after 90 days [6]. Counting from August 24, that puts the lapse around November 22, 2026. This is my calculation, not a date the register states, so the owner should confirm it. The contract renews January 31, 2027 [1].

## Halcyon Health: Tallgrass Survey Co.

Tallgrass Survey Co. provides post-visit patient satisfaction surveys by SMS and email. Its business associate agreement (BAA) is not executed. The draft arrived in August 2026 [4].

The open issue is data retention. Tallgrass wants to keep identifiable responses for 5 years for benchmarking. Halcyon will accept 18 months [4]. The Privacy Officer, Margaret Holloway, is due to send revised retention language by November 6, 2026 [4].

Other items holding things up:

- The security risk assessment was completed in September 2026 and passed with conditions [4].
- The signed order form is on hold until the BAA is executed [4].
- No PHI may be shared with Tallgrass before the BAA is signed, including test files or pilot data [4].
- In the meantime, Halcyon collects post-visit satisfaction for Juniper and in-person visits through the in-app survey [4].
- If the BAA is not signed by January 31, 2027, Quality & Patient Safety will look at other survey vendors [4].

## Summary

| | Northwind: Hollowpine | Halcyon: Tallgrass |
|---|---|---|
| Agreement | DPA | BAA |
| Blocker | Vendor wants to train its AI model on ticket content | Vendor wants 5-year retention of identifiable responses; Halcyon offers 18 months |
| Interim position | Operating under security exception; AI features off | No PHI shared; in-app survey used instead |
| Next date | Exception lapse around Nov 22, 2026 (calculated); renewal Jan 31, 2027 | Retention language due Nov 6, 2026; decision deadline Jan 31, 2027 |

**Halcyon's self-pay discount is bigger: 20% versus Northwind's 15%.** The two offers are different kinds of discount, though, so the dollar value depends on what you buy.

| | Northwind Labs | Halcyon Health |
|---|---|---|
| Offer | 15% off list for annual prepayment on a Growth plan [2][4] | 20% prompt-pay discount for self-pay patients who pay in full on the day of service [1] |
| Base | First-year contract value at list price [2][4] | Self-pay visit rates |
| Example saving | Growth lists at $1,200/month; the prepaid annual price is $12,240, down from $14,400, a saving of $2,160 a year [2] | New patient visit $165 → $132 (saves $33); established visit $120 → $96 (saves $24); annual physical $195 → $156 (saves $39) [1] (savings calculated from these list prices) |

**Conditions and exclusions**

Northwind:
- The 15% applies to annual prepayment on Growth; list prices and this discount are unchanged in the October 1, 2026 discount memo [4].
- Multi-year deals may add an extra 5% per committed year, capped at 10%. The sources don't say whether this stacks on the 15% prepayment discount, so confirm with sales before assuming a combined figure [2][4].
- Any discount above 15% goes through the deal desk and needs higher-level approval [4]. The 15% prepayment rate itself is a standard rate, not a negotiated one.
- Registered non-profits and accredited educational institutions get 50% off Growth automatically. The sources don't say whether this combines with the prepayment discount [2].

Halcyon:
- The 20% does not apply to vaccines or injectables, whose prices are already cost plus administration. For example, a COVID-19 vaccine is $140 and PCV20 is $265 [3].
- Sliding-fee patients (household income under 250% of the federal poverty level) get a 40–100% reduction in visit costs instead [1][3]. The sources don't say whether that combines with the prompt-pay discount.
- Self-pay patients who are not paying in full that day get no discount, and balances can be paid over up to 12 months interest-free for amounts over $200 [1][7].

**Bottom line:** On the headline percentage, Halcyon's 20% beats Northwind's 15%. Northwind's offer is worth more in total dollars because it applies to a much larger annual contract. Halcyon's discount is for a single visit, and it excludes vaccines and injectables.

**Tomás Herrera, Halcyon Health**
- He is the system steward for Revenue Cycle Management (RCM), which approves changes to RCM's clinical systems [15].

- He is the change approver for the Security team and must sign off on normal changes to services that store Restricted data [8][18].
- He owns the Customer data retention standard v2, which cut default archive retention to 365 days and shortened deletion requests to 14 days [17].
- He is the security reviewer on RFC-031 (persisting Tributary snapshots). His approval is still pending, and nothing ships to the private beta until he signs off [14].
- Leadership has asked Dmitri Sokolov to unblock the RFC-031 security review with Tomasz by the end of October [11].

**Are they the same person or related?**
No evidence suggests this. They work for different organizations in unrelated roles: Halcyon's Tomás runs revenue-cycle and scheduling work, and Northwind's Tomasz runs security. The only link is the similar first name. Your notes may simply have two contacts with similar names.

**Short answer:** At Northwind, the incident commander can approve an emergency change during a declared incident, and the owning team's change approver reviews it within two business days. At Halcyon, the on-call medical director can approve an emergency change to a clinical system, but only to stop ongoing patient harm, and the Clinical Systems Change Advisory Board (CSCAB) reviews it at its next meeting.

## Northwind Labs

**Who approves:** The incident commander (IC) can approve emergency changes, but only during a declared incident [8]. The IC is paged from a dedicated rotation when someone runs `/incident declare` [9]. Approval does not require the owning team's change approver, though the IC can approve changes that would normally need that person's sign-off [9].

**Review afterwards:**
- The owning team's change approver must review the emergency change retroactively within two business days [8]. Each team has one named approver and one delegate [10]. For example, Platform's approver is Oluwaseun Adeyemi, with Kofi Mensah as delegate [10].
- Every SEV-1 and SEV-2 incident gets a blameless postmortem within five business days of resolution, and these are reviewed at the Thursday reliability meeting [9].

**Skipping the canary bake:** If a fix must ship during an incident, the IC can approve skipping the canary bake with `/deploy expedite`. The expedite is logged in `#eng-changes` [11].

**Limits that still apply:** Rollbacks never need approval [12]. Friday deploys still need the on-call engineering manager's approval [11][12].

## Halcyon Health

**Who approves:** The on-call medical director may approve emergency changes to clinical systems [1][2]. The on-call rota is reached through the answering service at 555-0144, option 2 [1]. The policy limits emergency changes to those "to stop ongoing patient harm" [2].

**Review afterwards:** CSCAB reviews the emergency change at its next meeting [2]. CSCAB meets weekly on Wednesdays at 14:00 Eastern [2]. The policy does not set a fixed deadline for that review. CSCAB decisions are logged in the intranet change register, and changes made without the required approvals are reported to Quality & Patient Safety (QPS) as safety events [2].

**Other rules that still apply:** Any cutover that moves a job between runners or servers needs a written runbook explaining how double-running is prevented [2][6]. That rule came from incident IR-0412, in which two reminder runners were active at once [2][6]. Results-routing and patient-facing changes are "significant" changes that normally need the steward, a CMIO safety sign-off and CSCAB review [2][4].

## Key differences

| | Northwind Labs | Halcyon Health |
|---|---|---|
| Approver | Incident commander, during a declared incident [8][9] | On-call medical director [1][2] |
| Trigger | Declared incident [8] | Ongoing patient harm [2] |
| Post-review by | Owning team's change approver, within 2 business days [8] | CSCAB, at its next meeting [2] |
| Other review | Postmortem for SEV-1/SEV-2 within 5 business days [9] | Unapproved changes reported to QPS [2] |

Halcyon's policy does not say whether the CMIO's clinical safety sign-off is needed for an emergency change. It only lists the on-call medical director's approval and the CSCAB review [2]. The documents I found do not include a recorded emergency change, so I could not check how either process works in practice.
